body:
## Summary

Adds a new quick-intro workflow that allows staff to send a Cofactor AI introduction email to interested professionals with a single click from the signup notification email. The feature includes a dedicated view, template, and eligibility checks to ensure the email button cannot bypass the queue's filtering rules.

## Key Changes

- **New `ProConnectorQuickIntroView`** (`staff_views.py`): Implements the one-press intro flow behind staff login. GET previews the AI-drafted email; POST sends it immediately or queues it for business hours. Shares the same eligibility rules and atomic claiming mechanism as the main processing queue to prevent double-sends and filter bypasses.

- **New `quick_intro_block_reason()` function** (`proconnector.py`): Gate function that returns a human-readable reason why a record can't be introduced (already sent/queued/skipped, unsubscribed, or filtered as test/spam), or `None` if sendable. Ensures the email button respects all queue filtering.

- **New `proconnector_quick_intro.html` template**: Staff-facing page showing signup details, an editable email draft (auto-generated via AI), and two action buttons: "Send intro email now" (immediate) and "Send during business hours" (queued). Blocked records show their status instead of send buttons. Includes client-side double-submit protection.

- **Enhanced team notification** (`utils.py`): 
  - `notify_interested_professional()` now generates an HTML alternative with a prominent "Send the Cofactor AI introduction" button linking to the quick-intro page
  - New `_interested_professional_notification_html()` helper renders the HTML with proper escaping of all user-submitted fields
  - `notify_professional_signup()` accepts optional `html_body` parameter for HTML alternatives

- **New URL route** (`urls.py`): Added `proconnector_quick_intro` path for the quick-intro view.

- **Comprehensive test coverage** (`test_proconnector.py`, `test_pro_version_signup.py`):
  - `QuickIntroBlockReasonTest`: Validates eligibility checks for all blocking conditions
  - `QuickIntroAccessTest`: Verifies staff-only access and login requirements
  - `QuickIntroPageTest`: Tests GET rendering, draft generation, and blocked-record handling
  - `QuickIntroSendTest`: Tests POST actions (send/queue), validation, double-press protection, and error handling
  - Pro version signup tests verify the HTML notification includes the intro button and properly escapes user input

## Implementation Details

- The quick-intro flow uses the same `claim_email_for_send()` atomic claiming mechanism as the main queue, preventing concurrent double-sends even across views
- AI draft generation only happens when the record is sendable and no draft was posted (re-renders after errors preserve the user's edits)
- Already-sent records show their stored email body instead of paying for a fresh draft
- The send itself is a POST (not a GET), so mail scanner link prefetching cannot trigger an introduction
- All user-submitted fields in the HTML notification are escaped via `format_html` to prevent XSS
- Validation ensures the compensation disclosure is present in any edited email body before sending

author: jfolcini
body:
### #4128 — an attribute KEY could forge a second log record

`format_log_record` and `format_span` sanitized attribute *values* but wrote *keys* raw, so a newline in an attacker-controlled key split the tab-separated record and forged a second, legitimate-looking one for any downstream parser. `metrics_exporter`'s `write_attrs` already escaped keys — which is what makes this an omission rather than a design.

Both writers now escape the key through `sanitize_inline`.

**Review found the record separator was not the only one that mattered.** A tab in a key forges an extra **field**, which the original tests could not see because they asserted record count alone. Field counts are now asserted too, in both writers, across a hostile-key table: `\t`, `\r`, `\r\n`, a literal `=`, empty, all-whitespace, and 16 KiB.

The escape's **injectivity** is load-bearing and was untested: `sanitize_inline` replaces the backslash *first*, so a key containing a literal `\n` two-character sequence cannot be confused with an escaped newline on the way back. That ordering is now stated in the function's docs and pinned by an unescape round trip.

U+2028/U+2029 are deliberately left unescaped — the only reader splits on `\n` and `\t`, neither breaks on them, and escaping would alter legitimate body text. `format_span`'s `status={status:?}` stays exempt because `Status::Error`'s derived `Debug` escapes through `str`; that was an unstated assumption and now has its own test.

Every write site was enumerated rather than assumed: four line-writers exist, the other two already sanitized keys, and `otlp.rs` is protobuf-over-HTTP rather than a line format. No raw site remains.

### #4127 — a branch that could never fire, and a comment describing the wrong mechanism

`recent_errors_from_log_dir` looked for a plain `agaric.log` first. Production never writes that name: the appender uses `filename_prefix` with `Rotation::DAILY`, and `tracing-appender` renders that as `agaric.log.{date}` unconditionally — the bare name is `Rotation::NEVER` only, verified against the vendored crate source rather than the docs. Git history confirms **no released build ever wrote the plain name**, so there is no deployment to regress.

The dated file is now checked first, the plain one kept as a documented fallback for test fixtures, and the comment no longer describes logrotate.

The test writes **both** files with distinct markers on purpose: a weaker test would not have reddened, because the old fallback already found the dated file when the plain one was absent.

Closes #4127
Closes #4128

author: clentjewell
body:
Follow-up to #15/#16. `_tools/verify-deployed.mjs` still asserted the preview posture — `X-Robots-Tag: noindex` present, `robots.txt` disallowing everything, a fixed 10-URL sitemap, `/api/contact` returning `status: "preview"`. Run against the live site it reported **13 failures on a healthy deployment**, which is worse than having no checker at all: the next real failure gets waved through.

## Changes

- **Robots assertions inverted.** `EXPECT_NOINDEX=1` flips them back for a preview clone, so one tool covers both.
- **`balgadesigns.com.au` dropped from the WordPress-leftover pattern.** It was there to catch references back to the old WP site while we were on the workers.dev host; now it's the site's own domain and matched 30–40 times per page. Still catches `wp-content`, `wp-json`, `elementor`.
- **Sitemap check asserts the origin**, not a URL count that any content edit breaks.
- **`robots.txt` is read from our own section.** Cloudflare prepends a managed block containing `Disallow: /` lines, which was making the old "robots.txt disallow" check pass for entirely the wrong reason.
- **Contact probe no longer submits a real enquiry.** It sets the honeypot field, which the Worker accepts and discards without storing. Running this against production can't drop junk in the client's inbox any more. (The old version did — see the note below.)

## New checks, all things the go-live specifically put at risk

- per-page `<link rel="canonical">` must name this origin — the silent-ranking-loss failure mode
- `script-src` must still be hash-based, not fallen back to `'unsafe-inline'`
- HSTS present
- `/admin/` sends noindex
- `/_cms/csp.json`, `/cms-config.json`, `/review/` still 404 for signed-out visitors
- warns if something upstream is blocking AI crawlers (it currently is — see #15)

Exits non-zero on failure so it can gate something later if wanted.

## Verification

`node _tools/verify-deployed.mjs` against `https://balgadesigns.com.au` — 10 routes, security headers, 3 gated paths, 60 assets, 404, redirect, both contact probes, sitemap, robots, font caching: **all pass**, with the AI-crawler note firing as expected.

author: panghy
body:
## Summary

When intentd flushes multiple queued messages as one combined turn, it stamps a shared `queueInfo.batchId` on every drained user row (PROTOCOL §5.5). This PR makes the transcript render those rows as one delivery: the `ConversationTurnGap` between adjacent turns whose user messages carry the same non-empty `batchId` renders compact (`h-2`, the existing `compactOperationalSeam` scale) instead of the default `h-10` user gap.

## Changes

- `src/shared/types/agent-message.ts` — additive optional `batchId` on `MessageMetadata.queueInfo`.
- `src/lib/utils/queue-info.ts` — `getQueueInfo` now surfaces a non-empty string `batchId` (malformed/empty values are dropped without invalidating the rest); new dependency-light `isBatchedDeliverySeam(currentTurn, nextTurn)` helper: both user messages share the same non-empty `batchId` and the current turn produced no assistant output (adjacent rows only — no lookahead across assistant messages).
- `src/lib/components/chat/ConversationTurnGap.svelte` — new `batchedDeliverySeam` prop rendering `h-2` with `data-batched-seam="true"`. It takes precedence over the event-notification branches on both sides, so a batch mixing plain user messages and wake cards (agent-to-agent cards, PR-monitor/hook wakes, event notifications) compacts every internal seam.
- `src/lib/components/chat/ChatPanel.svelte` — computes the seam per turn boundary and passes it to `ConversationTurnGap`.

## Behavior preserved

- Message bubbles and the "Waited in queue" header are untouched — only the between-turn spacing changes.
- Rows without `batchId` (older daemons, single deliveries) render exactly as before; the field is additive.

## Tests

- `queue-info.test.ts`: `batchId` extraction (valid / absent / empty / malformed), `isBatchedDeliverySeam` (same id, different id, absent id, assistant output in between, wake-card metadata, orphan/last turns) — mock payloads mirror the PROTOCOL §5.5 shape.
- `conversation-turn-gap.test.ts`: batched seam renders `h-2` and wins over the `h-10` user gap and the wake-card branches on both sides; unbatched seams keep today's classes.

## Verification

- `pnpm vitest run src/lib/utils/__tests__/queue-info.test.ts src/lib/components/chat/__tests__/conversation-turn-gap.test.ts` — 26 passed.
- `pnpm run check` — 0 errors.
- `pnpm tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit`, `pnpm tsc -p tsconfig.main.json --noEmit`, `pnpm tsc -p tsconfig.preload.json --noEmit` — all clean.

Part of the batched-delivery grouping feature (daemon-side `batchId` stamping lands in intent-hq/intentd; this FE change is additive and safe to merge only after the intentd PR per the protocol-change merge order).

author: audumla
keevin-xu
body:
Fixes #3907.

Two problems in the `Reshape` arm of `candle-onnx/src/eval.rs`, both about a
`0` in the target shape.

`allowzero` was never read, so a `0` was always treated as "copy the
corresponding input dimension". With `allowzero=1` it should mean a literal
zero-length dimension.

Separately, the product that `-1` is inferred against skipped zeros. Under the
default `allowzero=0` a `0` copies an input dimension, so it is part of the
volume and belongs in that product; leaving it out made the inferred `-1` too
large. This one needs no attribute, and ONNX's own `zero_and_negative_dim` test
shape reaches it.

Resolving every non-`-1` dimension first fixes both, because the inference then
divides by the true product. While there I also rejected more than one `-1`,
which the previous shape of the code could silently accept.

Three regression tests using ONNX's own `Reshape` test shapes, plus one for
multiple `-1`s. All fail without the fix.

The `known == 0` guard rejects `-1` inference whenever the rest of the volume is
zero, which is broader than the spec sentence about `allowzero=1`. It also covers
a copied zero under `allowzero=0`, which onnx/onnx#6104 left unsettled. Rejecting
seemed better than dividing by zero, but I am happy to narrow it.

A case still left open: a negative other than `-1`, such as `[-2]`. ONNX specifies
inference for `-1` only; `onnx.reference` accepts any negative because it
delegates to `np.reshape`. This patch rejects them explicitly instead of casting
to `usize`, so behaviour is unchanged and only the message improves.

author: lbm364dl
body:
`validate_review_ledger` scopes arms A and B with

```python
pol = [r for r in rows if (r.get("unit_kind") or "") == "polity"]
```

and nothing validated that column. **Measured: typo'ing `unit_kind` on all 256 polity rows takes the checked
population from 256 to zero and the gate prints**

```
PASS: every banked verdict names a polity that exists
```

— its strongest claim, on no evidence. Same shape as #407 (guarded on a filename the repo does not contain),
#412 and #420, except here it is the gate's **scoping** rather than an arm, which is worse: every arm stays
individually correct while the population they run over disappears.

### Three changes

- **`unit_kind` vocabulary pinned** to `{match, polity, ingest}`. This column also separates assertion
  verdicts from polity decisions when banked work is counted — ignoring it produced a **55.4%** orphan rate
  against a true **15.7%** on #308, because 415 polity-level rows were counted as orphaned assertions.
- **A floor on how many rows the filter may select.** Not a pinned count — the population moves as work is
  banked — but it cannot legitimately be empty while the ledger holds 993 rows. This catches the filter
  emptying for *any* reason, including causes a vocabulary check cannot see.
- **The PASS message states its evidence**: `all 256 polity-keyed row(s) name a live polity; 993 ledger rows
  carry a known status and unit_kind`. A gate that reports how much it checked cannot make its strongest
  claim on nothing without saying so.

The selftest case typos **every** polity row rather than one, because one row leaving the population is a
quiet weakening and all of them leaving is the failure mode. Verified: exit 1, naming the floor.

### How I got here, and what I am not claiming

Generalising #477's status-vocabulary gap, I swept tracked tables for vocabularies that tools filter on but
nothing pins: **13 candidates**. Rather than file all 13 — my last sweep produced 21 findings and was wrong
about essentially all of them — I checked the one I had direct evidence for: `unit_kind`, which I had needed
hours earlier to correct my own #308 measurement. Its only filter turned out to be *inside this gate*, which
is what made it worth fixing.

**The other 12 are unverified and I am not claiming them.**

Gates 75 (unchanged), selftest 98 → 99. All 75 gates pass; full selftest green.

author: lazzyman
body:
## What this PR does

This PR separates Omni media upload configuration from model inference configuration. Operators can keep temporary media upload policy, credentials, and model selection on DashScope while routing chat completions to a self-hosted OpenAI-compatible Omni endpoint. The existing single-DashScope-configuration behavior remains the fallback when no dedicated upload channel is configured.

Omni activation now depends on a usable upload channel rather than the inference hostname. Both normal delivery and reactive re-upload use only the dedicated upload endpoint, credential, and model, with upload-cache identity independent of inference changes.

Successful media policy tools now return absolute result paths in their model-visible response, including every keyframe for multi-output extraction. The `read_file` declaration also advertises its existing audio and video support so the model can inspect generated media.

## Why it's needed

Previously, a self-hosted inference URL disabled Omni even when a valid DashScope upload channel was available, because activation and upload calls were coupled to the inference provider. Separately, edited media paths were only exposed as client artifact metadata, so the model could not reliably follow a clip or extraction with `read_file`; the tool declaration also hid its runtime audio/video capability.

## Reviewer Test Plan

### How to verify

1. Configure a self-hosted OpenAI-compatible inference model with explicit image/audio/video modalities, then configure `omni.delivery.upload.baseUrl`, `apiKeyEnv`, and `model` for DashScope. Attach a real video and confirm Omni is active, upload-policy and multipart requests use only the upload route/key/model, and chat-completion requests use only the inference route/key/model.
2. Let the model call a media editing tool. Confirm the following model request contains an absolute output path and `read_file` guidance, then call `read_file` on that path and confirm the derived media is uploaded and delivered again.
3. Exercise video clipping followed by video reading, and audio extraction followed by audio reading. Confirm both operations succeed and the `read_file` tool declaration presented to the model includes `audio, video`.
4. Omit one dedicated upload field or unset the named key environment variable. Confirm startup fails with an actionable configuration error and sends no upload request.
5. Leave all three dedicated upload fields absent under a static DashScope inference configuration. Confirm the legacy upload path remains active.

Local verification completed: 546 focused Core tests, the CLI nested-settings regression, full build, bundle, typecheck, lint, generated schema validation, and `git diff --check`. A bundled-CLI proxy E2E ran twice with real H.264/AAC media and real ffmpeg/tool execution: 5 inference requests, 1 upload-policy request, and 3 multipart uploads covering the source video, derived MP4, and derived WAV. A separate independent harness also passed.

### Evidence (Before & After)

Before: custom inference hosts failed the provider activation gate; successful media edits returned only a summary to the model; `read_file` did not declare audio/video support.

After: custom inference remains isolated from a dedicated DashScope upload channel; model-visible tool results include absolute media paths; `read_file` can be selected for both audio and video results.

### Tested on

|     OS     | Status |
| :--------: | :----: |
|  🍏 macOS  |   ✅   |
| 🪟 Windows |   ⚠️   |
|  🐧 Linux  |   ⚠️   |

### Environment (optional)

macOS, Node.js 22.23.1, ffmpeg 8.0.1, no sandbox. External DashScope and custom inference services were replaced by separate local HTTP protocol doubles so the CLI, sockets, multipart bodies, tool loop, media bytes, request routing, models, and credential boundaries could be inspected deterministically.

## Risk & Scope

- Main risk or tradeoff: the configured upload model must be accepted by DashScope, and the custom inference service must be able to resolve the resulting `oss://` resource while supporting the declared media modalities.
- Not validated / out of scope: live DashScope upload, live custom inference behavior, `audio_url`, and `use_audio_in_video` compatibility were not tested or changed.
- Breaking changes / migration notes: none. The new upload settings are optional; when any one is set, all three are required. API keys remain outside settings and are loaded through the configured environment-variable name.

## Linked Issues

N/A

## 本 PR 做了什么

本 PR 将 Omni 媒体上传配置与模型推理配置解耦。运维可以继续使用 DashScope 的临时媒体上传策略、凭据和上传模型，同时把聊天推理路由到自部署的 OpenAI 兼容 Omni 地址。如果没有配置独立上传通道，则继续保留原来由单套 DashScope 配置同时承担推理和上传的兼容行为。

Omni 激活条件现在依赖可用的上传通道，不再依赖推理地址的 hostname。正常媒体投递和服务拒绝后的响应式重传都只使用独立上传 endpoint、凭据和模型，上传缓存身份也不再受推理配置变化影响。

所有媒体策略工具成功后都会在模型可见响应中返回绝对结果路径，多产物关键帧提取会列出每一个结果。`read_file` 声明也补充了运行时已有的音频和视频支持，使模型能继续检查生成的媒体。

此前，即使存在有效 DashScope 上传通道，只要推理走自部署地址，Omni 也会因为激活条件和上传调用都耦合到推理 provider 而失效。另外，剪辑或提取结果的路径只存在于客户端 artifact metadata 中，模型无法可靠地继续调用 `read_file`；该工具声明也隐藏了实际已经存在的音视频处理能力。

## Reviewer 测试计划

### 如何验证

1. 配置一个显式声明 image/audio/video modalities 的自部署 OpenAI 兼容推理模型，并为 DashScope 配置 `omni.delivery.upload.baseUrl`、`apiKeyEnv` 和 `model`。附加真实视频，确认 Omni 已激活，上传 policy 和 multipart 请求只使用上传路由/key/model，聊天推理请求只使用推理路由/key/model。
2. 让模型调用媒体编辑工具。确认下一次模型请求包含绝对输出路径和 `read_file` 指引；随后对该路径调用 `read_file`，确认派生媒体被再次上传和投递。
3. 分别验证视频剪辑后读取视频、音频提取后读取音频。确认两条链路均成功，并且模型实际收到的 `read_file` 工具声明包含 `audio, video`。
4. 缺少任意一个独立上传字段，或取消所引用的 key 环境变量。确认启动以清晰配置错误失败，并且没有发起上传请求。

本地验证已完成：546 个 Core 定向测试、CLI 嵌套配置回归、完整 build、bundle、typecheck、lint、schema 生成校验和 `git diff --check`。使用真实 H.264/AAC 媒体、真实 ffmpeg 和真实工具执行的 bundle CLI 代理型 E2E 连续通过两次：5 次推理请求、1 次上传 policy 请求、3 次 multipart 上传，覆盖源视频、派生 MP4 和派生 WAV。另一套独立 harness 也通过。

### 前后对比证据

改动前：自定义推理地址无法通过 provider 激活条件；媒体编辑成功后模型只收到摘要；`read_file` 没有声明音视频支持。

改动后：自定义推理与独立 DashScope 上传通道隔离；模型可见工具结果包含绝对媒体路径；模型可以为视频和音频结果选择 `read_file`。

## 风险与范围

- 主要风险或取舍：配置的上传模型必须被 DashScope 接受，自定义推理服务必须能够解析返回的 `oss://` 资源，并支持所声明的媒体 modalities。

author: jrajahalme
body:
Network policies may contain hundreds or thousands of HeaderMatch or TLS rules referring to a small set of Secrets. Each reference previously constructed a separate SecretWatcher or Envoy TLS ContextConfigImpl, including its SDS provider callbacks and other context state.

Add separate weak caches for SecretWatchers and upstream and downstream TLS contexts, keyed by the SDS name or Cilium TLSContext protobuf, respectively. Reuse a live context when an equivalent policy configuration is encountered.

Reset the caches together with the policy maps after an NPDS stream restart, preserving the existing agent-restart behavior. Prune expired cache entries asynchronously after policy updates and worker quiescence, keeping pruning off the policy-update hot path.

Benchmark an NPDS update containing 1,000 policies that reference the same SDS-derived CA validation context. The CA is delivered through a real dynamic SDS provider rather than embedded in the policy TLS contexts.

Optimized benchmark results (3 repetitions):
```
                                CPU time     Retained heap     Heap/policy
  TLS context cache enabled     1.47 ms      1.581 MiB         1.619 KiB
  TLS context cache disabled    3.95 ms      4.990 MiB         5.109 KiB
```
This reduces CPU time by approximately 63% and retained heap by 68%, saving about 3.41 MiB per 1,000-policy update and increasing throughput by 2.68x.

The benchmark uses Envoy's small, single-certificate test CA. Production SDS resources commonly contain larger CA bundles comparable to those shipped with operating systems, so the benchmark likely understates the memory impact of retaining duplicate certificate-related context state.

Benchmark results for deduplication of SecretWatchers on HeaderMatches are more modest (duplicating header sized secrets carries less overhead), but are still positive around 20-25% for CPU and memory.

author: ksharma-xyz
body:
## What

Refreshes an open Park & Ride card on a repeating beat while the rider is watching it, instead of
answering "can I still get a space" once on the tap that opened it.

## Changes

- `pollWhileCardsAreOpen` in `ParkRideRefreshHelper`: runs the refresh on an interval behind two
  gates, both of which must hold.
  - The screen is being looked at: gated on the screen's own subscriber count through
    `SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed` per `docs/POLLING_LIFECYCLE.md`, so backgrounding stops the
    loop and returning restarts it, with the subscription grace keeping it alive across a
    rotation.
  - At least one card is open: `collectLatest` restarts the wait whenever the open set changes,
    so collapsing the last card ends the loop and opening another begins a fresh interval.
- The interval is the shared per-facility cooldown from Remote Config. A tick spends nothing on
  its own: `refresh` is the same call the tap makes and the cooldown still decides which
  facilities are actually fetched, so asking more often could not produce a newer number.
- `SavedTripsViewModel` starts the loop from the open-card set.
- `docs/POLLING_LIFECYCLE.md` register gains a row for
  `ParkRideRefreshHelper.pollWhileCardsAreOpen`.
- `PollingLifecycleGuardTest`'s member regex listed only the visibility modifiers and
  `override`, so any other soft keyword before `fun` stopped the match and the flow was
  attributed to `File.?`, a name no register row can match. `pollWhileCardsAreOpen` is the first
  `suspend fun` here to hold a `WhileSubscribed`, which is why nothing caught it earlier; the
  remaining soft keywords are listed alongside `suspend` so the next one does not repeat it.

## Testing

- New `SavedTripsParkRidePollTest` covers: no poll with no card open, polling at the configured
  cadence while one is open, the loop stopping when the last card closes and when the screen is
  no longer collected, and a fresh interval on reopening
- `./gradlew :feature:trip-planner:ui:testAndroidHostTest --continue` green
- `./gradlew detekt --continue` green

body:
Initial **`@miragon/bpmnlint-plugin-rules`** — a bpmnlint plugin bundling the standard structural rules, the Camunda 7/8 deployability rules and a few Miragon BPMN conventions behind one resolver. Extracts the lint composition from `Miragon/bpmn-modeler` and replaces `emaarco/bpmnlint-plugin-agentic`.

## Two ways to use it (both verified end to end)

**Classic bpmnlint plugin** — `.bpmnlintrc` + the CLI:
```jsonc
{ "extends": ["bpmnlint:recommended", "plugin:@miragon/rules/recommended"] }
```
```bash
npx bpmnlint diagram.bpmn
```

**Programmatic** — a self-contained resolver over every layer (no `bpmnlint` install, works offline):
```ts
const linter = new Linter({
  config: getDefaultLintConfig({ engine: 'c8' }),
  resolver: createBundledResolver(),
});
```

## Highlights

- Three Miragon rules (`no-generated-ids`, `element-id-naming`, `flow-through-element`), **off by default**; element sizing delegated to bpmnlint's `standard-size`.
- `bpmnlint` is a **peerDependency**; the Camunda + structural rules are bundled.
- **Upstream-drift guards** — `camunda-sync` (referenced-rule list + newer-engine-config tripwire) and `bpmnlint-sync` (built-in rule list) fail CI when a bundled layer moves.
- TS + tsup (ESM/CJS; rules emitted as bare-CJS factories for the classic path), MIT, CI (`ci` job, Node 22), release-please with OIDC publish.

## Quality gate

`typecheck` · `lint` · `format` · `knip` · `dependency-cruiser` · `vitest` (48) · `build` · **tarball distro smoke** (drives the real bpmnlint CLI + resolver in a throwaway consumer) — all green.

## Notes

- Base `main` is an empty initial commit, so the diff is the whole package.
- Follow-ups (other repos): migrate the modeler onto this package; archive `bpmnlint-plugin-agentic`.
- Camunda engine rules via classic `.bpmnlintrc` are partial (need `camunda-compat` resolvable + moddle extensions); the programmatic `getDefaultLintConfig({ engine })` wires them fully.

author: ngonie69
body:
Adds a **Delivery route** filter to the POD upload report, built from the 2026 routes workbook with every business partner code resolved against SAP.

## What changed

- **Route filter** on `/pod-report`, beside the existing currency/uploader/location filters. Routes are labelled with the day they run (`BORROWDALE (Tue)`), and a **Not on a route** option surfaces shops the workbook never placed on a truck.
- **Route pill** under the card code on each row, so a filtered list is self-evidencing.
- **`Delivery Route` column** on all invoice sheets of the Excel export (Product Invoices, Crate Invoices, Pending PODs, Uploaded PODs) — which also reaches the scheduled POD report email, since it attaches the same workbook.
- **`scripts/DeliveryRoutes/generate_delivery_routes.py`** — regenerates the catalogue from the workbook.

## Why the catalogue is generated, not transcribed

The workbook's own code column cannot be used as it stands. Checked against the SAP customer master:

| Problem | Count |
|---|---|
| Codes naming no partner in SAP | 28 of 120 |
| Stops with no code at all, only a name | 119 of 239 |
| Codes naming the **wrong shop** | 1 |

Most bad codes are currency-suffixed codes written bare — the sheet says `spa059`, SAP holds `SPA059 USD`, and **the space is part of the key**. The wrong one is `tmp013` "TM CHIREDZI", which SAP holds as *TM Budiriro* in Harare — a different shop in a different province. The name is right and the code is wrong, so the generator resolves names and treats codes as hints.

It also takes **every currency variant** of each shop. "Spar Bridge" is `SPA002`, `SPA050 USD` and `SPA070`; an invoice carries whichever matches its currency, so listing one would silently drop the others. Note the currency lands in the code inconsistently — `SPA050 USD` carries a suffix, `OKZ104` ("OK Hwange USD") does not — so variants can't be derived from the code.

Same inputs reproduce `DeliveryRoutes.g.cs` byte for byte. Hand-resolved stops live in the generator's `OVERRIDES` dict, so the run stays reproducible and the reasoning sits next to the data.

## Validated against production

Checked 2026-08-20 against the live company (`Kefalos Cheese Products NEW`):

- **All 347 distinct partner codes exist in production.** Zero missing.
- **70.1% coverage** of POD-eligible invoices across 57,028 invoices since 2026-05-01; **67.8%** over the report's default 30-day window.

**The unrouted third is mostly not a mapping gap.** Over that 30-day window, 1,031 POD-eligible invoices are on unrouted partners, and they break down as:

| | invoices | share |
|---|---|---|
| Food-service / trade accounts (Simbisa Brands, Vales & Saini Icecream, Absolute Refrigeration, Crispy Chicken, Maid & Mate) | ~823 | 80% |
| Bulawayo-region shops (PnP Bradfield/Gwanda/Ascot, TM Jason Moyo, Greens) | 208 | 20% |

The first group looks like accounts the trucks don't serve as route stops at all. Within the second, the workbook lists only "CHEESEMAN BULAWAYO" for that route, consistent with those shops being served off the Bulawayo depot. There's also a small residue of real retail shops the 2026 sheet never lists (Spar Bonsa, PnP Hypermarket, Greens George Silundika) — **worth a look if those should be on a route.**

> An earlier revision of this description said the remainder was *mostly* Bulawayo. That came from a sample my own paging had truncated at 2026-07-10; the figures above are from the full window. Commit 4bb3758 corrects the same claim in the code comment.

## Reviewer notes

- **Membership, not a label.** A shop can be on two routes — AMP Meats is on both `PNP NORTH` and `CBD2`. The Cheeseman depots all invoice to `CHE020`, so that one partner belongs to all four routes that reprovision a depot. Flagging in case you'd rather the depots came out.
- **Route is derived in the Web, not added to the DTO.** The API caches the report as a JSON blob for up to `RetentionDays`; a new DTO field would read back `null` from every cached snapshot until it aged out.
- **61 stops** (Kariba/Mutare hotels, lodges, safari camps) are in no SAP customer master at all, so they can never reach a report. The generator prints them on every run.

## Verification

- **1,979 tests pass**, 28 of them new (`DeliveryRouteCatalogueTests`).
- The Excel column is **inserted** after Card Code rather than appended, shifting every column after it across three sheets. A test reads the produced workbook bytes back to confirm nothing shifted out from under its header.
- The page was driven in both light and dark with **no console errors**. Note the live drive ran against local dev, which points at `KEFALOS_TEST_3` — a near-empty test company — so it exercised the control, the menu and unrouted detection, but no named route filtered rows. Named-route behaviour is covered by the unit tests and by the production validation above.

body:
The cycle count is already parsed out of every simulation into `TestResult.runtime_cycles`, and
`run_and_assert_test` then drops it. This surfaces it in the PyTest output and, on GitHub Actions,
collects it into a table on the job summary page.

## Added

- A `Performance Summary` block at the end of every PyTest run, listing each test's runtime in cycles.
- The same table appended to `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` when running under GitHub Actions, so the numbers
  are on the check page without opening the log.

## Changed

- `run_and_assert_test` prints `[deeploy-perf] runtime_cycles=N` for each simulation, before the
  assertions so a failing test still reports its cycles.

## Notes on the implementation

Collection happens in `pytest_runtest_logreport`, which fires on the xdist master for every worker's
report. All CI jobs run `pytest -n 4`, so a module-level list filled inside the tests would stay in
the worker process and never reach the summary; scraping the captured stdout on the master is what
makes the four workers' numbers land in one place.

`pytest_terminal_summary` does run in the workers as well, each holding only the tests it ran, so
writing the job summary is guarded to the master. Without that guard the shared summary file gets one
partial table per worker plus the complete one — five tables for a four-way run.

Tests on platforms that report no cycles (Generic, XDNA2) contribute no rows, and a run with no cycle
data at all prints nothing.

## Verification

Real GAP9 tests through gvsoc, `-n 2`:

```
============================= Performance Summary ==============================
  [PASS] test_platforms.py::test_gap9_kernels[Kernels/FP32/Add/Regular]            972 cycles
  [PASS] test_platforms.py::test_gap9_kernels[Kernels/Integer/Add/Regular]       6,257 cycles
  [PASS] test_platforms.py::test_gap9_kernels[Kernels/Integer/MatMul/Regular] 4,066,151 cycles
  [PASS] test_platforms.py::test_gap9_kernels[Kernels/Integer/Pad/Regular_1D]     7,263 cycles
```

| Test | Status | Runtime (cycles) |
|---|:---:|---:|
| `test_platforms.py::test_gap9_kernels[Kernels/FP32/Add/Regular]` | :white_check_mark: | 972 |
| `test_platforms.py::test_gap9_kernels[Kernels/Integer/Add/Regular]` | :white_check_mark: | 6,257 |
| `test_platforms.py::test_gap9_kernels[Kernels/Integer/MatMul/Regular]` | :white_check_mark: | 4,066,151 |
| `test_platforms.py::test_gap9_kernels[Kernels/Integer/Pad/Regular_1D]` | :white_check_mark: | 7,263 |

Also checked: serial (no `-n`) gives the same table; a failing test still contributes its row; Generic
tests contribute none.

No workflow changes — GitHub sets `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` for every step, container jobs included.

## Summary

Completes the `node-<format>-newsdesk` series: `node-psd-newsdesk` gains react-psd-app's second rendering path, **Anime2.5DRig motion mode**, next to the existing static PSDTool mode.

- `avatarMode: auto | static | motion` mirrors the React app's decision flow: run the rigger first, use motion when a normalized `face` part is found, else fall back to the unchanged pure-Node static renderer; forcing `motion` on an ineligible PSD surfaces the rigger's diagnostic.

The sibling example's MIT rigger + WebGL renderer are bundled **read-only from source** — no copies, no React changes; Anime2.5DRig attribution reproduced in README en/ja.
- Per-frame audio input drives `mouthOpen` via the renderer's documented lip-sync path; the renderer has no direct eye input, so its internal blink automation runs deterministically under `blinkSeed` (documented in diagnostics + README).

author: muzi131313
body:
## 背景

MG 用户反馈 `getD2c` 方法在资源名包含中文时存在问题：

- 下载后的文件名中中文字符被替换成下划线；
- HTML 中仍引用原中文文件名，导致图片路径与磁盘文件不一致；
- 图片文件扩展名与真实格式不一致。

## 根因

`src/tools/get-d2c.ts` 的 `writeResource` 使用 `[^a-zA-Z0-9_-]` 清洗文件名，将中文等非 ASCII 字符全部替换为下划线；同时 HTML 在资源落盘前写入，未同步重写资源引用。

图片格式错误来自 `data:image/*` 分支只根据 key 的扩展名落盘，未从 MIME 或文件魔数推断真实格式；对象类型的资源被 `JSON.stringify` 后按 base64 写入，也会产生错误内容。

## 变更

- 保留中文等 Unicode 文件名，仅清理路径分隔符和 `./..` 目录穿越片段。
- 资源先落盘，记录「原始 key -> 最终文件名」映射，再据此重写 HTML 引用后写入 HTML。
- 资源内容解析按优先级推断扩展名：data URL MIME > HTTP `content-type` > 文件魔数嗅探 > key 扩展名。
- 新增 `src/tools/get-d2c.test.ts` 覆盖中文文件名、路径清洗、扩展名推断、引用重写等场景。
- `package.json` 测试脚本纳入新测试文件。

## 文件变更

| 文件 | 说明 |
|---|---|

author: michaelwautier
body: First slice of [PLAN.md](../blob/main/PLAN.md). No gameplay yet — this puts the foundation in place and proves the loop, the coordinate system, and the render pipeline all work end to end. ## What's here **Deterministic core.** `Rng` (mulberry32) is seedable, serializable, and cloneable. Everything in the simulation will draw randomness from it, so a match is fully reproducible from its seed. That matters twice over: encounter math becomes unit-testable, and Phase 4 can re-simulate league fixtures headlessly with the same engine you play against. **Fixed-timestep loop.** The simulation advances in whole 1/60s ticks regardless of display refresh rate, so a 144Hz screen behaves identically to a 60Hz one. Rendering gets an `alpha` to interpolate between the last two ticks, so motion stays smooth. Frame delta is capped at 250ms to avoid the spiral of death when a backgrounded tab returns. **Pool geometry.** `core/pitch.ts` holds the sphere pool as world units — a circle of radius 50, goal lines at ±46 with a 7-unit half-height mouth — plus the helpers (`clampToPool`, `isInGoalMouth`) the match engine will need. **Renderer.** Canvas 2D, DPR-aware, drawing entirely in world units via a single transform. Geometry in the renderer matches `core/pitch` exactly, so no call site converts coordinates by hand. **Debug overlay.** fps, ticks, match clock, ball position and speed. Toggle with `~`. **CI.** Typecheck, tests, and build on every PR. ## Note on the bouncing ball `core/match/state.ts` currently simulates one ball loose in the pool. That's a deliberate placeholder — it establishes the contract the real engine will use (a pure, seeded `step` over plain state, with previous positions recorded for interpolation) and gives the renderer something moving to prove interpolation works. Phase 1 replaces its contents with the actual match state machine. ## Verification - 23 tests passing across RNG, pitch geometry, and simulation (determinism, ball containment, speed conservation through bounces). - `tsc --noEmit` clean under strict mode with `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` and `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`. - Production build succeeds; dev server transforms and serves every module. - Confirmed running in a browser: pool, halfway line, centre circle, both goals with nets and posts, and the ball all render as intended. Across two samples the clock advanced 0.53s → 0.82s and the ball moved (6.7, 9.6) → (10.2, 14.8) with speed conserved at 22.0 u/s, so the fixed-timestep loop and interpolation are live. fps settles at 63; no console errors. ## Next Phase 1: rosters, player movement and AI positioning, and the pause-and-menu encounter system — the milestone where you can play a full match against the Luca Goers.

Two independent changes from the residual backlog (maintainer-directed):

1. **Scope signal, observability only** (docs/issues/swarm-runaway-growth.md failure mechanism 4, chosen as a signal rather than enforcement): when a swarm member touches a file outside its recorded working directory, the swarm coordinator gets one deduplicated, non-urgent boundary-delivered message naming the member, its root, and the first outside path. Never blocks or rejects the operation; members without a recorded working_dir are exempt. Lives in its own module (server/file_scope_signal.rs) wrapping the existing bus touch-record path; dedup is once per member (the signal means 'this member leaves its scope — look', and the first outside path is included). 2. **Comm e2e flake** (docs/issues/comm-e2e-tests-flake-under-saturation.md): the worker corrected the issue's diagnosis — the test-env lock is acquired before the clocks start, so lock contention was NOT the mechanism; setup (server/agent construction) competing for CPU inside the timed sections under full-suite parallelism is. ## Summary

author: guangyu-reflexio
body:
## Summary

`StorageConfig` is an untagged union, and `StorageConfigSQLite` was its only member with no required fields and no `extra` restriction. That made it a catch-all: any payload failing the stricter members landed there instead of raising.

Measured against the real schema, **before** this change:

| stored blob | resolved as | should be |
| --- | --- | --- |
| supabase missing `db_url` | **SQLite** (url/key/schema dropped) | error |
| supabase missing `key` | **Postgres** (connects anyway) | error |
| supabase with empty-string `key` | **Postgres** | error |
| `{"nonsense": 1}` | **SQLite** | error |
| full supabase | Supabase ✅ | ✅ |
| `{}` | SQLite ✅ (OSS local default) | ✅ |

The first row is how a managed tenant ended up pointed at a local SQLite file: its storage object had no `_rpc`, a background sweep raised every few seconds for a week, and the resulting error volume exhausted the Sentry quota fleet-wide (org 56, 2026-08). The second row is arguably worse — it *succeeds*, connecting by a path nobody intended.

## Changes

**1. `extra="forbid"` on the SQLite, Supabase and Postgres members.** A config that loses or misspells a field now raises instead of changing backend.

**2. `validate_stored_config` validates `storage_config` strictly, before the lenient pass.** This is the fix that actually reaches production, and it is easy to miss:

```python
return Config.model_validate(normalized, extra="ignore")
```

`extra="ignore"` **cascades into nested models**, so it overrode the members' `extra="forbid"` entirely. Change 1 alone was cosmetic on the only path that mattered — every stored config is loaded through this function. Schema-evolution leniency for `Config`'s own retired fields is preserved; it just no longer extends to reinterpreting which storage backend an org is on.

**3. `type` is now a declared field on the SQLite and Supabase members**, matching what `StorageConfigPostgres` already did — accepted on input, `exclude=True` on output.

- *Accepting* it is required: the config API emits `type`, so tightening the models without it made an unmodified `/get_config` → `/set_config` round trip fail with a 422.
- *Not serializing* it keeps the persisted document byte-identical. The boot-time config upgrade rewrites every org's blob, and this change has no business altering what it writes.

An empty payload still resolves to SQLite on purpose — that is the OSS local-mode default in `local_file_config_storage`.

## Verification

- **20 tests** in `tests/models/test_storage_config_union.py`, covering the union adapter, the `validate_stored_config` load path, the type-tag round trip, and the unchanged serialized shape.
- **Mutation-verified**: reverting each of the four guards individually turns the suite red. My first version of these tests asserted only against the union adapter and passed while the real load path stayed broken — the `validate_stored_config` cases exist specifically because of that.
- OSS unit tier: **4893 passed**.
- **Checked against production before landing**: all 29 managed orgs carry one identical 6-key shape with no extra keys and still resolve to `StorageConfigSupabase` under the new schema; the 2 self-host orgs carry `None`. Nothing is rejected. Blast radius is zero.

## Related

Paired with the enterprise-side change that closes the path which produced the malformed config in the first place, and refuses SQLite for a platform-managed tenant.

## Note for the reviewer

This branch is stacked on `5e186cc1` ("filter playbook search by source"), which is the commit enterprise `main` currently points at but which is **not yet on this repo's `main`** — it lives on `origin/codex/explain-interaction-source-field`. Branching off `main` instead would have reverted that feature on the enterprise side. Once that PR merges this should rebase cleanly; if it squash-merges, this branch needs `rebase --onto`.

  * Prevented invalid configurations from being interpreted as a different storage type.
  * Preserved valid backend settings during configuration loading and serialization.
  * Continued supporting omitted values and retired top-level fields where applicable.

* **Tests**
  * Added comprehensive coverage for SQLite, Postgres, and Supabase configuration validation and round trips.

Run Flake8 and ESLint/Prettier on the GitHub-hosted runner instead of through Docker Compose.

body:
## Summary
Follow-up to #985 / issue #987. Instead of disabling PassKey wallets on Brave entirely, offer them through external hardware security keys, which is the one PRF path Brave actually supports:

- New `PrfSupportMode` (`'platform' | 'security-key' | 'none'`) replaces the boolean probe internally. Brave reports `'security-key'`: its platform passkey provider drops PRF, but Chromium's FIDO stack (which Brave keeps) speaks CTAP2 `hmac-secret` to external authenticators (YubiKey and similar).
- `registerWebAuthnCredentialWithPrf()` pins `authenticatorAttachment: 'cross-platform'` in `'security-key'` mode, so the browser only offers authenticators that can actually deliver PRF — the platform provider can never accept the credential and silently drop the extension (the orphaned-passkey failure mode from #987).
- Onboarding security step (`StepSecurity.vue`): on Brave the PassKey tile is shown with a "Security key required" chip and hint instead of being hidden — but password remains the preselected default, since the user may not own a hardware key. Platform-mode UX is unchanged.
- `isPrfSupported()` keeps its boolean contract for existing callers (cold-key import, MPC passkey) and now returns true on Brave.
- Unlock/evaluation paths need no changes: `credentials.get()` with the stored credential id already lets the browser prompt for the security key.
- New i18n keys in `us.ts` + `de.ts`.

## Test plan
- [x] `test/webauthn-prf-support.test.ts` extended to 6 tests: mode detection (platform / security-key on Brave / none / brave-probe-error fallthrough) plus registration attachment pinning (`platform` off Brave, `cross-platform` on Brave).
- [x] ESLint clean on all touched files.
- [x] `npm run build:web` passes (SFC parse gate).
- [x] Full vitest: only failures are the known pre-existing crossDevice real-timer flakes (different test each run; all pass in isolation; no import path from this change).
- [ ] Manual on Brave with a YubiKey: create PassKey wallet, lock, unlock via security key.

The oneAPI releases are usually on the latest LLVM versions. So this should be useful for not just the closed source Intel compiler as well.

[build] In file included from /home/krasznaa/ATLAS/projects/acts/acts/Core/src/EventData/PrintParameters.cpp:12:

author: ssamy-wlm
body:
## Summary

- `.github/workflows/supabase-migrations.yml`: `check-prod-current` has been permanently red on every PR since it was built — the CLI pipeline it depends on was never bootstrapped (no `SUPABASE_DB_URL` secret, migration ledger never reconciled — see CLAUDE.md's "Open items"). It's a read-only dry-run that's currently pure noise, not a real signal about any given PR's changes, so it no longer blocks/reddens PRs. A comment explains why and exactly how to re-enable blocking later.
- Updated the file's header comment to reflect this.
- `apply-on-merge` is **untouched** — confirmed byte-identical to `main`.

## Implementation note: continue-on-error had to go on the STEP, not the job

The instruction as given was to add `continue-on-error: true` to the job. I did that first, pushed it, and checked the actual resulting PR check via the GitHub API rather than assuming — **it still came back `conclusion: "failure"`**. Job-level `continue-on-error` only keeps the overall *workflow run* from failing and lets `needs.<job>.result` read `"success"` for any downstream job; it does **not** change that job's own check-run conclusion, which is what actually shows up as red/green on the PR.

Moved `continue-on-error: true` onto the "Dry-run against production" *step* itself instead — that's what actually converts a failing step into a successful job conclusion. Verified again against a real run: the step still executes, still hits its real `exit 1` (SUPABASE_DB_URL is unset, so the underlying dry-run genuinely fails, exactly as it would have before), but the check now reports `conclusion: "success"`. Confirmed via the check's actual job log that this is the real result, not a skip — it's now genuinely informational-only rather than silently skipped.

## Optional item: not implemented

Tried the optional graceful-skip-on-missing-secret guard on `apply-on-merge` too (`if:` referencing `secrets.SUPABASE_DB_URL`), but confirmed with `actionlint` that the `secrets` context isn't available in job-level `if:` conditions at all (only `github`, `inputs`, `needs`, `vars` are). Doing this properly would require adding a second job just to check-and-output whether the secret is set, then gating `apply-on-merge` on `needs.<that-job>.outputs.x` — real added complexity, not a one-line guard. Since the ask was explicitly "only if that doesn't complicate the file," left `apply-on-merge` exactly as-is instead, per the primary instruction.

## Verification

- `python3 -c "import yaml; yaml.safe_load(...)"` — valid YAML.
- `actionlint` (installed fresh for this check) — no issues on the final file.
- Diffed the `apply-on-merge` job block against `origin/main` directly — byte-identical.
- **Live-verified on this PR's own checks**, not just read as YAML: fetched the actual check run via the GitHub API after each push. First attempt (job-level) came back `failure`; corrected version (step-level) came back `success`, with the job log confirming the underlying script still ran and still hit its real failure condition — it's genuinely marked non-blocking, not skipped or faked.

This is a workflow-only change — no app code, no data, no migrations.

- [ ] `apply-on-merge` continues to behave exactly as before once merged to `main`
- [ ] Sarah's confirmation

Trois changements demandés par Benji, et un trou trouvé dans le garde-fou en les appliquant.

## 1. L'ordre du menu suit l'ordre de lecture

« Offres & tarifs » était listé avant « Réalisations » alors qu'il pointe 27 points de page plus loin — le premier item envoyait à 62,1 %, le second à 34,9 %. Un menu d'ancres annonce un parcours ; il mentait en l'annonçant dans un autre ordre que celui qu'on lit.

Corrigé à la source, donc barre desktop et menu mobile d'un coup. Un avertissement est posé au-dessus de la liste : tout changement d'ordre dans `Home.tsx` doit être répercuté ici — c'est exactement ce qui venait de se produire avec le déplacement des logos.

## 2. Approche avant les offres

L'offre est la demande ; tout ce qui la précède construit le dossier. Réalisations = la preuve, Approche = comment je travaille, Offres = combien. Poser le prix avant la méthode revient à demander de l'argent avant d'avoir expliqué le travail.

Va dans le sens du compte rendu Adel × Benji, [10:58] : « tu demandes déjà un engagement alors que t'as pas fini de convaincre ». Le tarif reste accessible tôt par le hero, dont le diagnostic dit que la place est juste.

Menu et page concordent, strictement croissants : Réalisations 34,9 % → Notre approche 62,1 % → Offres & tarifs 70,5 % → Contact 87,3 %.

## 3. « Mon approche » → « Notre approche »

⚠️ **Va contre F-08 du diagnostic**, qui recommande d'assumer le « je » partout — « le je est ici la position forte, pas la position modeste » — et inverse la correction du matin même (« Notre action » → « Mon action » dans les cartes). Le site remêle donc les deux personnes sur ce point.

Décision de Benji, donc inscrite en **exemption explicite** dans `check-diagnostic.mjs`, avec son motif et sa date, plutôt que laissée en angle mort. Le contrôle F-08 reste actif partout ailleurs.

## Le trou du garde-fou

Le contrôle F-08 est resté vert sur ce changement, alors qu'il aurait dû échouer. Il recomposait le texte de `main` puis des frères de `<body>` ne contenant pas `main` — or l'app monte header, main et footer dans un même `<div>`. **Il ne voyait ni l'en-tête ni le pied de page**, et annonçait F-08 conforme sans les avoir jamais lus.

Il lit désormais `document.body.innerText`. Deux effets immédiats : il a vu les deux « Notre approche » (en-tête et pied, même clé i18n), et il a révélé que la tolérance du bandeau cookies ne couvrait que son début — « analyser notre trafic » la faisait échouer. La phrase entière est maintenant tolérée.

## Vérifications

- `build:prerender` exit 0 · `check:offer` 5/5 · `check:diagnostic` 6/6 · axe-core 0
- Menu et sections mesurés strictement croissants, les huit entrées

author: gregdhill
body:
The FAQ, Refunds and Deep Dive pages still described the pre-intents protocol. Checked each claim against the `bob-gateway` codebase and rewrote what no longer holds.

## FAQ

Removed both of the leading questions:

- **"Who pays the gas fees?"** — the Relayer no longer estimates gas (it only submits SPV proofs). Gas is estimated by the solver at quote time, priced in USDT and withheld from the fill. That's already documented on the Fees page, so the entry went rather than getting rewritten.
- **"What happens if my DeFi action fails?"** — custom strategies were removed; the API rejects `strategyTarget`/`strategyMessage` on every version with `CustomStrategyNotSupported`.

Replaced with a single **"What happens if my swap fails?"** covering the BTC-to-X retry/re-quote/refund path and the X-to-BTC escrow reclaim.

## Refunds

- BTC-to-X failures refund **BTC to the order's `refundAddress`, or USDT on Ethereum** — there is no wrapped-BTC fallback (`crates/solver/src/onramp.rs:340`).
- X-to-BTC orders escrow **USDT**, not wrapped BTC (`USDT_ADDRESS` is the only allowlisted token in `GatewayOfframpRegistryV6.s.sol:85`).
- The second failure case is now the destination swap or bridge reverting, since user-supplied strategies no longer exist.

## Deep Dive

Rewritten end to end. The old page had solvers holding wrapped BTC, the Relayer issuing quotes and creating orders, and a Bitcoin Light Client verifying the BTC-to-X direction.

- **BTC to X** — API-signed quote (1-minute validity, echoed back on `create-order`), deposit address from the solver's own Bitcoin wallet, TRM screening plus destination-call simulation, then one atomic `releaseFundsAndCallStrategy` on `GatewayOnrampV8` with destination gas withheld from the fill.
- **X to BTC** — USDT escrow in `GatewayOfframpRegistryV6`, `keccak256(orderId, registryAddress)` OP_RETURN commitment, SPV-verified `finalizeOfframpOrder` against `LightRelay`, and the owner's unilateral `refundOrder` after `refundDelay`.
- Added controls and contracts tables, and replaced both mermaid diagrams.

### One call worth reviewing

The page now states plainly that **only X-to-BTC is SPV-verified**. BTC-to-X settles on Bitcoin confirmations — the deposit lands in the solver's own wallet — and the user's protection is the signed quote plus the automatic refund path. That matches the contracts (`GatewayOnrampV8` has no relay reference; only the offramp registry validates proofs), but it's a more conservative claim than the marketing pages make. Reword if you'd rather frame it differently.

## Not included

`overview.mdx` has related staleness left untouched: step 2 says a solver "locks the output asset in a smart contract... before the user sends any Bitcoin" (no such lock — the solver EOA stays custodian until release), and step 4 plus the Non-Custodial accordion apply Light Client verification to the flow as described. Happy to do those in a follow-up.

## Verification

`pnpm run build` and `pnpm run lint` pass in `gateway-docs/`.

author: adity1raut
body:
## Summary
Fixes #3368 — a `PostureExceptionPolicy` with no `Resources` set is documented and implemented as "applies everywhere" for manual-review controls, but silently does nothing at all for resource-backed findings on the identical control ID.

## Root cause
`matchingControlExceptions` (`core/pkg/opaprocessor/processorhandlerutils.go`) already implements the convention explicitly:

```go
// no resources = no scope constraint, matches any cluster
if len(policy.Resources) == 0 {
    matches = append(matches, policy)
    continue policyLoop
}
```

But for resource-backed findings, the vendored `opa-utils` `exceptions.Processor.GetResourceExceptions` does the opposite:

```go
for _, resourceToPin := range ruleException.Resources { // zero iterations if Resources is empty
    ...
}
```

An exception with an empty `Resources` list is matched against zero resources — it never applies. Same exception object, same control ID, opposite outcome depending only on whether the control happens to be manual-review or resource-backed. No error or warning either way; the exception just looks like it's working and silently isn't.

## Fix
The real fix belongs in the vendored `opa-utils` matching loop, but that's a separate repository. This PR adds a narrow, additive workaround entirely within kubescape: `resourceScopedExceptions`, called once per resource immediately before `SetExceptions`, gives every scope-less exception a `resourceID` designator naming that specific resource — evaluated by the exact same `compareResourceID` path `opa-utils` already uses for any other resource-scoped exception.

Since a scope-less exception currently matches **zero** resource-backed findings, this can only add a match where there was none before — it cannot change the outcome of any exception that already resolves correctly today. Exceptions that already carry a `Resources` scope are returned unchanged.

Note: `core/pkg/opaprocessor/processorhandlerutils.go`'s `updateResults` carries a `// This is a critical function - DO NOT CHANGE` comment. This change is intentionally minimal (one line swapped in the call to `SetExceptions`, plus a new, separately-testable helper function) specifically because of that — happy to adjust the approach if maintainers prefer it done differently.

## Test plan
- [x] `TestResourceScopedExceptions` — unit tests for the helper: nil input, already-scoped passthrough, scope-less gets a designator, mixed scoped/scope-less only touches the scope-less one, original slice element not mutated.
- [x] `TestUpdateResults_ScopeLessExceptionSuppressesResourceBackedFinding` — end-to-end regression through the real `updateResults` path: a scope-less exception now suppresses a matching resource-backed failing control (previously it silently did nothing), and a scope-less exception for an unrelated control ID still does not suppress this one.
- [x] Verified the new end-to-end test actually catches the bug: reverted the one-line fix locally and confirmed the test fails with the exact symptom from the issue, then reapplied the fix and confirmed it passes.
- [x] `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, and `go test ./...` (both modules, including `httphandler`) all pass with no regressions.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **Bug Fixes**
  - Resource-specific exception policies now correctly apply to findings even when the policy does not explicitly specify a resource.
  - Existing resource-scoped policies continue to behave as expected.
  - Unrelated control exceptions no longer suppress resource-backed findings.
  - Control skip/include filters now correctly determine rule exclusions, with whitelist behavior taking precedence.

- **Tests**
  - Added coverage for resource-specific exception matching, policy preservation, and control-based filtering.

More importantly, I turned it into the kind of baseline you were getting at. The new record explicitly captures:

mathematical consistency ≠ physical plausibility ≠ observational support
successful gravastar formation occurs on a fine-tuned separatrix
the authors themselves describe each successful configuration as “infinitely tuned”
the model uses homogeneous dust, spherical symmetry, a de Sitter interior and specific junction conditions
it produces a horizonless gravastar, not evidence for a baby universe living inside an already-formed black hole
it provides no evidence that our universe actually originated this way
it can therefore serve as a negative control for speculative-physics claims and headline inflation

I also encoded your 9/10 observation carefully. Sabine's rating is stored only as non_claim_calibration_only, with explicit instructions that it is not a truth score, confidence score, proof status, or evidence against the mathematics. Since the video appears to be brand new and I couldn't yet reliably pin its exact public YouTube ID, I did not invent one. The repository records the transcript as owner-supplied public commentary with the locator still unpinned.

I also upgraded the machine layer with the guard:

MATHEMATICAL_CONSISTENCY != PHYSICAL_PLAUSIBILITY != OBSERVATIONAL_SUPPORT

and added a general_relativity_black_holes_or_speculative_physics retrieval route, so this example can actually be pulled when Sabine-GPT is evaluating wild-but-mathematically-legal constructions. That feels particularly useful for the “the equations permit it, therefore Nature did it” genre of theoretical physics. 😆

## Summary by Sourcery

Establish a calibrated gravastar reference that helps prevent mathematically permitted models from being treated as physically or observationally established claims.

New Features:
- Add a calibrated adjacent-literature record for gravastar formation and its implications for speculative-physics claims.
- Add retrieval support for general-relativity, black-hole, and speculative-physics evaluations.

Enhancements:
- Strengthen epistemic safeguards by distinguishing mathematical consistency, physical plausibility, and observational support, and by isolating non-claim calibration ratings from truth or evidence assessments.

Build:
- Refresh generated research context, source fingerprints, timestamps, and projection metadata to include the new literature record.

Chores:
- Update public source records with the pinned arXiv v2 and journal DOI for the gravastar paper without attributing it to Sabine's publications.

## Summary

#15 put every single a member missed on the under band. That is wrong for a member who was on hiatus: they were taking part in no group activity at all, and the chart showed them as having performed the under song.

Wikipedia's 楽曲の選抜・福神 table distinguishes the two, and this uses it for Nogizaka.

## Reading the source

The table's legend separates the cases: `◎` center, `○` fukujin, `▲` selected, a **blank** cell meaning participation in a non-title track — under — and named states for absence: `休止`, `活動休止`, `不参加`, `辞退`, plus `未加入`, `卒業`, `契約終了` for outside the member's tenure.

Extraction needed colspan expansion. A single `卒業` cell spans every remaining single, so without expanding it the columns misalign and markers land on the wrong singles — the first parse produced 13 members for a 16-member single before that was fixed.

Filtering to absences **between** a member's first and last participation leaves the real interruptions: **16 members, 20 singles**. 生田絵梨花's 9th is one of them — the chart previously drew it as under, and it is the case that prompted this.

## In the chart

A single marked absent gets no point, the line breaks either side of it, and a faint vertical rule marks the interruption, so a break reads as absence rather than a missing segment. Hovering or tapping the rule gives the reason — `第9張《夏のFree＆Easy》 休止`.

Other groups have no data of their own here and are untouched.

## Verification

Driven in Chromium against a mocked Firestore. 17 checks here, plus the under, trajectory, tuning, drag, layout, formation, backfill, Nogizaka-edit, picker, edit, roster, panel, backup and regression suites: 299 checks, all passing, no page errors.

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| Dataset | 16 members |
| 生田絵梨花 9th | `absent`, reason 休止; no under point |
| Her line | two segments, both solid |
| Interruption | one rule, hit-testable via `elementFromPoint`, reports the reason |
| 山下美月 23rd | `不参加` |
| 北野日奈子 20th | one interruption |
| Members with no hiatus | one unbroken line, no rules |
| Hinatazaka / Sakurazaka / Keyaki | no rules — unchanged |

Two existing suites picked 生田絵梨花 as their gap example; they now select a member whose gap is genuinely under, so both cases stay covered.

author: stephieed
body:
Traite la cause des pertes du run `32302557156`. **Corrige aussi mon diagnostic précédent**, qui était faux.

## Le vrai mécanisme

En mode écrasement, la fusion additive ne protège plus rien. Une **sous-collecte** peut échouer sans que le profil écrit n'ait l'air anormal — identité introuvable, endpoint en panne, archive indisponible — et il part avec un champ simplement vide, qui remplace le bon.

| profil | perte | ce que portait le profil écrit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `jean-luc-melenchon` | 18 721 amendements, 1 016 votes, 33 textes | « identité introuvable » |
| `bruno-retailleau` | 36 textes portés | « votes introuvables » |
| `marine-le-pen` | 23 textes portés | **aucun avertissement** |

Le troisième cas est le plus instructif : ses amendements (13 991) et ses votes (1 813) sont **intacts**, seuls ses textes portés sont tombés, et **rien dans le profil ne le signalait**. Un garde-fou conditionné à la présence d'un warning ne l'aurait pas vu. Un garde-fou raisonnant sur le profil entier non plus.

## Mon diagnostic précédent était faux

J'avais attribué ces pertes à la publication d'un job **annulé** et au `if: always()` de l'étape de publication. Vérifiable, et faux : le profil de Mélenchon a été écrit à 21:13:30, **deux minutes après le lancement**, bien avant l'annulation de son job ; celui de Le Pen ne porte aucune trace d'interruption.

L'entrée de journal correspondante porte désormais un avertissement qui renvoie à la nouvelle. Ce qui y reste juste : le constat chiffré, la restauration, et la remarque sur la transposition abusive du principe de #443 — elle vaut, elle n'explique simplement pas ce cas.

## La règle

> Une collecte **vide** ne remplace jamais une collecte **non vide**. Champ par champ, pas profil par profil.

**Ce n'est pas une invention.** #427 l'a énoncée pour les gouvernements, et le code le dit noir sur blanc : *« distinguer "zéro dossier constaté" de "collecte incomplète" ; sans elle, l'appelant écraserait des profils avec un `textes: []` qui n'a jamais été mesuré »*. Les profils étaient le seul endroit à ne pas l'appliquer.

**Ce qu'elle ne bloque pas** : une correction de clé. #440 a remplacé 2 018 amendements par 944 — une baisse de plus de moitié, légitime, non bloquée : 944 n'est pas zéro. Seul le passage à **zéro** est refusé. C'est ce qui distingue ce garde-fou d'une demi-fusion, laquelle rendrait toute correction impossible et recréerait le défaut de #450.

**Et jamais silencieuse** : sans `--autoriser-collecte-vide`, la préservation est imprimée. Une préservation muette ferait croire la collecte réussie — ce serait un autre défaut.

## Deux couches, pas une

| | quand | attrape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ce garde-fou | à l'écriture du profil | la collecte ratée, avant qu'elle ne touche le disque |
| contrôle de perte (#461) | avant le commit | le reste — baisse partielle, profil disparu |

Aucune ne remplace l'autre : une baisse de 2 035 à 5 votes n'est pas un vide, et seul le contrôle de perte la verrait.

## Tests, vérifiés dans les deux sens

12 nouveaux — 9 unitaires sur la fonction, 4 de bout en bout reproduisant le scénario réel (profil committé complet, collecte vide, `--no-merge`).

Sans le correctif : **`assert 0 == 1016`** — les votes disparaissent, exactement comme le 19/08. Avec : tout est préservé, et une collecte non vide écrase toujours normalement.

`1621 passed`. Les 2 échecs de `tests/test_gouvernement_roster.py` sont antérieurs, documentés en #457.

## Ce que ça ne corrige pas

Le `if: always()` de la publication reste en place, et c'est maintenant un **choix** : puisque la destruction ne venait pas de là, publier le travail d'un job préempté reste utile. La question de marquer un artifact de job annulé comme partiel se pose toujours, mais sans l'urgence qu'on lui prêtait.

Les 38 pertes résiduelles de #465 — 49 textes portés, ~355 mandats — ne sont pas traitées ici : celle-ci empêche les prochaines, pas celles déjà subies.

author: sam-vrgl
body:
Closes #14.

### 1. The texture scale parameter that was never implemented

`renderer.js` passed a scale factor to `createSatinTexture`, which takes two parameters. JS swallowed the third silently.

The consequence was real. The canvas transform works in **millimetres**, so a pattern built from a bitmap is measured in millimetres too — a 40-**pixel** velvet tile became a 40-**mm** tile, magnified by whatever the output scale happened to be. Roughly 4x on screen, nearly 12x at 300 DPI. Blocky output on the one thing people actually print.

The tile now keeps its size in mm while the bitmap behind it is built at the output scale and mapped back down with `pattern.setTransform`. Three details:

- **Bitmap sizes round up to a power of two**, capped at 512. A zoom gesture walks through a continuum of scales; without quantising, every frame would allocate a canvas and run `Math.random` over all of it. With it, there are at most a handful of cached tiles per colour.
- **Velvet noise is per bitmap pixel, satin's sheen scales with the bitmap.** They need opposite treatment: noise should stay around one grain per output pixel at any scale, which is what resolution-independent means for a texture; the sheen is a shape, so it scales to keep the same physical width and comes out crisp rather than resampled.
- **The moivre call site left `dpr` out** of the scale it passed, understating it by half on any retina screen. `draw()` now computes the output scale once and hands it down.

### 2. Grid culling

At 4x zoom on a 700 mm ribbon the grid emitted **815 segments** into one path to show **38 mm** of design. The mode where precision matters was the slowest one.

The visible range is read back off `ctx.getTransform().inverse()` rather than recomputed from state, so it cannot disagree with the transform that was actually applied. Same view now costs **73 segments** — an 11x drop.

### 3. `toBlob`

`toDataURL` encodes synchronously and then base64-inflates the result by a third into a single JS string. The bigger problem is that mobile Safari handles very large `data:` URLs on `<a download>` unreliably, and the phone is where this tool is mostly used. The export canvas backing store is released afterwards rather than left for the collector — tens of megabytes at 300 DPI.

`downloadUrl` folded into `downloadBlob` on the way past: its documented reason for existing was a caller already holding a `data:` URL, and that caller was this export.

### Verification

**17 assertions in headless Chrome**, and the earlier suites re-run green: 40 (#6), 25 (#16), 32 (#12), plus the startup smoke test.

The texture assertions measure the property rather than the implementation, which took two attempts to get honest:

- **Blockiness** is mean absolute difference between adjacent output pixels, with the old behaviour reconstructed in the test as a control. **0.63 before, 4.91 after.** My first metric — counting distinct colours — was useless, because the noise only has 26 levels by construction and passed either way.
- **Tile size** is five satin stripes across 60 mm, checked at print scale, screen scale and 20x zoom. That is what proves the tile is still 12 mm rather than 12 px.

`after` lands at 4.91 rather than the theoretical 8.3 because a 472 px need rounds up to a 512 px tile, so the texture is slightly oversampled — the right direction to round.

Culling is checked against the uncalled baseline computed in the test (73 vs 815, with 38 mm of 700 mm visible), and separately that rendering twice produces identical pixels, so nothing about the picture changed.

Export: `toDataURL` is never called, a `blob:` URL reaches the anchor, the blob is a real `image/png` of real size, the object URL is revoked exactly once, the filename is unchanged, and a second export still works after the first zeroed the canvas.

### Still needs a human

**Export at 300 DPI and look at the velvet and satin.** The harness can prove the grain is there and the tile is the right size; whether it looks like fabric is a judgement only you can make. Velvet in particular now has a finer grain than before at print resolution — that is the fix working, but it is a visible change to how the material reads.

Worth testing the export on a real iOS Safari too, since that is the failure `toBlob` is meant to address and headless Chrome cannot show it.

author: defenwycke
body:
Published and live: https://bitcoinghost.org/docs/mining-discovery.md

Closes one of #402's acceptance criteria — "genesis signer set published" — which had nothing behind it.

## The set was verified before publishing, not sampled

The MPC elder set is the root of trust a miner-side shim verifies node-list checkpoints against. Publishing a set even one node disputed would be publishing a **wrong root of trust**, which is worse than publishing nothing.

Checked against **all eight nodes**:

```
sha256(sorted set) = 06d1d5a1cd930c33a978694910c862637be54689005b762bfa3c0b28d7cbfeda
8 elders, identical on vm1-vm8
```

(vm7 timed out on the first attempt and agreed on retry — a timeout, not a disagreement.)

The page tells readers to check it themselves against any node, and says that if a node disagrees with the page, trust the node.

## It states the status plainly

`MESH_NODE_LIST_CHECKPOINT_HEIGHT` is still `u64::MAX`. No checkpoint is proposed or served, and the shim has nothing to verify yet. The page says so up front rather than implying the feature works — the signer set is published now because it is stable and independently verifiable today, and it is the same value that will anchor the chain once discovery is armed.

It also states two things that are not flattering and are true:

- **Taking the set from a web page is weaker than compiling it in.** The first fetch is trust-on-faith; only after it are you on the signed chain. The page recommends `--genesis-file` from a source you already trust.
- **Three independently operated seeds do not exist.** Every pool node is run by one operator, so a shim seeded only with Ghost nodes trusts one party for its first fetch. Code cannot fix that.

## Also deployed

`hazync.md` — registered in the docs nav but never shipped, so its nav entry would have 404'd.

⚠ `hazedproof.md` and `node-reward-convergence.md` exist in the repo but are registered in **neither** the nav nor the `VALID` list, so they remain unreachable. Left alone rather than guessed at.

## Deployment note

The live `docs/index.html` had diverged from the repo (live kept an older "Full spec" footer link; the repo had added the hazync entry). I diffed before overwriting, backed up the live file to `index.html.bak.20260820-095831`, and verified the result by fetching through the public URL rather than trusting the upload.

body:
## La causa dell'intermittenza, ed è una lettera

Il sito linka `pixeldrain.net/`**`d`**`/<id>`. Il riconoscimento cercava `pixeldrain.net/`**`u`**`/<id>`.

L'indirizzo era **scritto nella pagina** a ogni tentativo, e il codice non lo vedeva. Il sintomo era indistinguibile da un clic andato a vuoto, ed è la ragione per cui le versioni 22 e 23 hanno lavorato sui clic senza mai toccare la causa.

## Le due forme non sono intercambiabili

Ognuna ha il suo endpoint per i byte, misurato sui due titoli della traccia del 2026-08-20:

| pagina | byte | esito misurato |
|---|---|---|
| `pixeldrain.net/d/<id>` | `pixeldrain.net/api/filesystem/<id>` | `206`, `video/mp4`, `Accept-Ranges: bytes`, 121 MB e 168 MB |
| `pixeldrain.net/u/<id>` | `pixeldrain.net/api/file/<id>` | `404 not_found` sugli stessi identificativi `/d/` |

Cioè: riscrivere una forma con l'endpoint dell'altra non darebbe un errore riconoscibile, darebbe un link che sembra morto. Per questo la mappa fra le due sta nel codice invece di un `replace` di comodo.

## Come è saltata fuori

Dalla diagnostica `PLAY hosts` aggiunta nella 23, e per un'ipotesi **diversa** da quella che si è rivelata giusta: era stata scritta per il caso 'questi titoli stanno su un altro host'. Quello che ha riportato non era un host nuovo, ma lo stesso host in una forma che il riconoscimento non conosceva, mentre la riga accanto diceva `url? none`.

Due righe che si contraddicono sulla stessa pagina. È il motivo per cui quella diagnostica resta anche adesso che l'ipotesi che l'ha generata è caduta, e il commento nel codice lo dice.

## Verifica

Le regex sono state provate sulle stringhe reali della traccia prima della build: i due indirizzi `/d/` del log, la forma `/u/` (che non deve regredire), e i casi che non devono agganciare (hanime.tv, Discord). Gli endpoint riscritti restano riconosciuti dall'intercettazione. Le risposte `206` sono state misurate su tutti e due i titoli, non su uno.

## In più, e non è codice

Il README di radice guadagna come si riconosce un **blocco di rete**, che non è un difetto di queste estensioni e va escluso prima di cercarne uno: un errore di connessione verso `[::1]` significa che il nome è stato risolto a localhost e la richiesta non è mai uscita dall'apparecchio.

## Summary
- New essay: *Interest Rate Derivatives: The Cut the Market Already Priced In* — covers FRAs, interest rate swaps, rate futures, and caps/floors/swaptions as FICC's largest product family, framed around how a Rates desk hedges or positions ahead of a central bank's recession-era rate cuts.
- Slotted into the "Derivatives & Funding" essay series between Convexity and Credit Spread, since it builds on the swaps/futures/forwards/options mechanics and bond rate-risk essays already there.
