author: alexander-shamray
body:
Appendix C's PR-25, and the last mandatory row in the plan. Three commits,
each self-contained.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Closes** | M6 — *deployable, observable and gated* |
| **Depends on** | PR-20, PR-22, PR-17 (all landed) |
| **New ADR** | ADR-022 — the canary is a second release, weighted by replicas |
| **Suite** | 795 tests, green: 18 architecture + 606 unit + 171 integration |
| **Gates** | licence, scaffold (81), observability, helm (all assertions), pipeline (27), coverage (10), canary (43) |

## What changed

**`ci:` path-filtered builds, staged tests, and the gates that say they ran**

§15.1's pipeline had one `dotnet test` pass, no path filter and no image build.
It now has the fork, three stages, and a gate whose subject is whether each
stage exists at all.

**Three stages are three new ways to select nothing.** `dotnet test` exits
**zero** on a filter that matches no test — §12.1's oldest trap — so splitting
one run into three multiplies the ways to be green and empty. The quality gate
`docs/testing.md` asked for is here, and it is more than the floor that callout
described: the floors sit well under the measurements, because a number in a
file goes stale and what they grope for is an order-of-magnitude miss. The half
with no number in it does the work — **every test project in `Platform.slnx`
ran in some stage, no stage was empty, and no test ran in two.** That last one
turns `ci.yml`'s "exhaustive and disjoint by construction" from a claim into a
check; on the integration stage an overlap is a container set paid for twice.

Two inventories are gated the same way: every immediate child of `src/` and of
`src/Services/` must be matched by some path filter — §15.1's own instruction,
and the check that would have caught `src/Gateway/**` and `src/BFF/**` being
deployables CI never rebuilt — and every Dockerfile under `src/` must be built
by some matrix entry, in both directions. The third check there is the one
neither direction can see: a matrix entry reading
`needs.changes.outputs[matrix.filter]` on a name no filter defines evaluates to
the empty string rather than erroring, so the step is skipped and the job goes
green having built nothing.

The per-service image build closes a gap `compose.yml` names by hand — that
smoke is filtered to `deploy/compose/**`, so a Dockerfile broken by a source
change surfaced on the *next* compose pull request rather than on the offending
one.

**`feat(deploy):` a canary that is a second release, weighted by replicas**

§15.5 specified a canary in four sentences and named no machinery, so building
the rollout is what forced the choice. The canary is a second Helm release of
the same chart whose pods answer to the same Service, so the share it serves is
`canary / (stable + canary)`.

**The rejected option is the one every reader reaches for first, and it is
disqualified by topology rather than taste.** An nginx-style ingress canary
annotation splits traffic at the Ingress, and this platform has exactly one —
the gateway's. Everything behind it is dialled by Kubernetes Service name from
§10.2's route file and from `PricingHop.cs`, both of which hold those names as
literals *on the stated grounds that the host is the Service name*. So an edge
weight can canary the edge and **cannot canary Catalog or Ordering at all**.

**`docs:` record PR-25 in the plan, the roadmap and the repo guidance**

Appendix C's row gains the six things found by building it; the roadmap closes
M6; `docs/pr-decision-log.md` gains PR-25's block; `CLAUDE.md` carries the live
rules — the phase, three tree entries, the suite count, the stage split, the
next free ADR number, and three lessons that travel.

## Four things were found by building it

**`service.version` cannot tell the two tracks apart.** The resource already
carries a version attribute, so the design looked finished before it was
checked. `BuildInfo.Version` strips the source-revision suffix deliberately —
its own comment argues a value changing every commit turns one series into
thousands — and §4.4 pins no assembly version, so **every host in this platform
reports `1.0.0`**. Registered, exported, separating nothing: §13.6's own trap in
a new place. `deployment.track` through `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES` replaces it,
and **no production C# changed** — the SDK's resource builder already honours
that variable, established by a test against an exported resource rather than by
reading the documentation.

**§15.5's first rung is not expressible at the replica count §15.3 ships.** At
`replicaCount: 3` a single canary pod already takes 25% — five times the 5% the
chapter asks for. The requested weight is therefore a **ceiling**: `plan`
returns the largest canary that stays within it and refuses where even one pod
overshoots, naming the 19 stable replicas that would satisfy the step. Rounding
to the nearest expressible weight was the one-line alternative and is the whole
failure mode — a step labelled 5% serving five times the blast radius anybody
authorised. `autoscaling.maxReplicas` is 20, which is exactly 19 plus one
canary.

**The weight arithmetic was wrong in floating point at that very input.**
`19 * 0.05 / 0.95` evaluates to `1.0000000000000002`, so `ceil` bought two pods
and served 9.5%. Not an exotic input — the first step of the default plan.
Found by the test asserting that the function naming the required replica count
and the function checking it agree, which turned out to be catching two bugs at
once: the two had also been written to opposite rules.

**A flag added for one gate moved another gate's input.** `--logger trx` is how
the stage gate counts, and it changes where the coverage collector writes: each
stage then leaves the run's merged attachment **and** one partial per test
project. `domain_coverage.py` asserted exactly one file, correctly, when it was
written. It now merges — with `max` over a key that reproduces the collector's
own `lines-valid` exactly, so reading the same attachment twice cannot inflate
the figure. The union is worth having: 253 lines from the unit stage, 192 from
the integration stage, **257** from both.

## The honest cost

**Nothing here has reached a cluster.** No environment, no kubeconfig, no
registry. `deploy.yml` is `workflow_dispatch` only, because a deploy on `push`
would fail on every merge and a pipeline red by design trains everyone to
ignore it. This is the platform's **third artefact of that kind**, after PR-23's
charts and PR-24's alert rules. The deciding is tested; the acting is four
commands nobody has run.

**The premise underneath the mechanism is unmeasured.** kube-proxy spreads
*connections*, not requests, so keep-alive, HTTP/2 multiplexing to the gRPC
listener, or a client that opens one connection and holds it will each
under-deliver the weight. Nothing short of a cluster can measure that, and
ADR-022 records it as owed rather than implying otherwise.

**A decision was taken rather than deferred, and it can be argued with.** §12.9
and `docs/testing.md` both read *"a threshold that fails a build is PR-25's
quality gates"* — which defers rather than promises — while the same sentence
argues that a diagnostic wired to a build failure stops being read and starts
being satisfied. Both cannot be honoured. **The threshold is declined on §12.9's
own argument**, and the three sites saying it was owed now say it was declined,
so a later change arguing for one is arguing against that paragraph rather than
filling a gap it left open.

**One breaking change to the charts, taken now because it is free now.** The
Deployment's `matchLabels` gains `app.kubernetes.io/track`, and that field is
**immutable** — adding it to an installed release is a delete-and-recreate. It
costs nothing today because nothing anywhere has installed these charts, and it
would cost a downtime window later.

**Signing is not implemented.** §15.1's node reads "Build + sign images"; images
are built and not signed, because signing needs a registry and a key this

author: poggufanz
body:
Patch release cleaning up the passive hook lane — the path that runs at every prompt, on every command, without the user typing anything. No new command, no new record type, no schema change.

## What changes

**Bash hook no longer writes over your prompt.** `__rocky_precmd` spawned the handler detached without setting `ROCKY_HOOK_SPEECH_FILE`, so `speakTty` took the immediate-write branch and wrote straight to the tty device from a disowned process — unordered against the shell's prompt draw and the user's own keystrokes. It now claims a per-spawn speech file, and drains it at the next prompt. This mirrors the mechanism `rocky-hook.ps1` has used since 0.5.2; the TypeScript side needed no change, because `index.ts` already calls `flushHookSpeech()` in a `finally` for both handlers.

Session ownership is enforced: a name is recorded before the spawn, and only names this session claimed are ever printed. Two terminals sharing one `$ROCKY_HOME` never print each other's messages.

**No more deep-memory hint on typos.** A repeated misspelling no longer asks you to wrap the misspelling in `rocky run`. Detection is exit 127 alone — Bash sends it natively, and `rocky-hook.ps1` now reports it for `CommandNotFoundException`, captured alongside `$LASTEXITCODE` so Rocky's own suppressed `$Error` entry cannot mask it.

Only command-not-found is covered. A missing *file* (`cat nofile.txt`, exit 1) is indistinguishable from an ordinary failure without stderr, and the passive handler never receives stderr. Recorded rather than quietly dropped.

**`rocky hook status` discloses a stale hook.** Hook protocol moves to 0.4.0, with a test asserting both assets carry the constant. Installing the package does not rewrite `~/.rocky/rocky-hook.*`, so without this line the Bash fix would ship and never reach an existing install. `status` stays read-only.

## Rejected approach, recorded

An earlier commit on this branch detected typos by probing `PATH` for the command's first token. That is wrong on PowerShell in the ordinary case: cmdlets, functions, and aliases live in the shell's command table, never on the filesystem, so `Get-Item` classified as a typo and silenced a real hint. It was caught by two failing real-host smokes in `hook-powershell.test.ts` and replaced with the host-authoritative 127 signal. `src/core/path-lookup.ts` was removed with its last caller.

## Test plan

- [x] `npm test` — one failure, `setup-health` "expired graceful cleanup force-kills only the owned child", a known timing flake under suite load; `setup-health` is untouched by this branch and the preceding run was fully green
- [x] `hook-powershell` real-host smokes pass on both Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7.x
- [x] Focused gates: `path-lookup` (since removed), `hook-handlers`, `hook-speech`
- [x] WSL Bash smoke lane
- [x] Release-truth / package-metadata / documentation tests
- [x] Manual check on a real interactive Bash session after merge: message lands on its own line above a clean prompt, typing is not interrupted, a second terminal never prints the first one's message, and `~/.rocky/hook-speech/` does not accumulate files

Prompt ordering cannot be proven by any pipe-based harness — that limitation is why the defect survived this long. The automated tests prove the mechanism; the ordering needs the manual check.

author: benzsevern
body:
A running `rmem-mcp` and a `rmem` invocation against one `memory.json` lost each other's writes. Both crates named the limit; neither closed it.

## The fix is not the one the notes predicted

`rm-mcp` said it meant *"a lock file, not a reload-per-call"*. That was wrong twice over. The failure is a **lost update**, not a torn file:

```
A: load ................................ save   <- writes what it read
B:        load ... change ... save              <- and this is gone
```

Both saves are individually fine. B's change is lost because A's snapshot predates it and A never looked again. A lock around `save` alone would have faithfully serialised writing that stale snapshot over B's work — it would have looked like a fix and not been one.

Reloading without a lock narrows the window. Locking without reloading doesn't close it either. **Only both together do.**

So `store` gains `with_write` / `with_read`, holding the lock across the whole read-modify-write and handing the caller an `Engine` that cannot outlive it. A closure rather than a pair of functions a caller brackets by hand, because an engine outliving its lock *is* the stale snapshot above.

`rm-mcp` stops holding an engine across calls — that was the bug, not the optimisation it resembled. It now pays the snapshot parse and index rebuild per tool call deliberately, on a turn that has already spent hundreds of milliseconds on an embedding API. Same trade as exact search over an ANN index.

## Three decisions worth reviewing

**An OS advisory lock, not a create-and-delete lock file.** The obvious implementation strands a user after any crash: the file outlives the holder, every later run refuses against a process that no longer exists, and recovery means documenting "delete this file" — which they will then do while a real holder is running. The kernel drops an advisory lock on close, panic, `SIGKILL` and power loss alike. Checked rather than assumed, before the design was chosen: a holder killed with `SIGKILL`, lock file still on disk, releases it to the next process.

**A sidecar file, not the store.** `save` replaces the store through a rename, so a lock held on it is a lock on an inode the next save unlinks — the second writer would lock the *new* file and both would believe they were alone. There's a test for exactly this.

**A bounded wait, not an indefinite one.** Every holder is doing milliseconds of work, so 5s means wedged rather than busy, and blocking forever turns one stuck process into two. Past the deadline: a refusal that says nothing was written.

## No new dependencies

`File::lock` / `try_lock` are std, stable since 1.89, and `TryLockError` separates contention from a broken lock **in the type** rather than leaving it to an `ErrorKind` comparison. The cost is an MSRV bump from 1.85 to 1.89 — stated, because it is the trade. The alternative was `fs4`, which is four crates for something the standard library now does.

## Tested under contention

The `rm-cli` spec set the bar: *"a lock that is not tested under contention is worse than an honest limitation."* That standard is met rather than avoided.

- Exclusion, and the refusal naming what happened and that nothing was lost
- Shared readers not queueing behind each other; a reader waiting for a writer, and vice versa
- The lock surviving a `save` (the sidecar property)
- A failing closure writing nothing and freeing the lock
- A bracket over a store that doesn't exist yet
- **A second real process** (`crates/rm-host/tests/locking.rs`) — spawned, refused, then killed, with the lock confirmed released. The child takes its lock through the standard library rather than through `rm_host`, so the test cannot pass by both sides sharing a mistake.

## Docs

Every note claiming this limit is corrected rather than left to mislead: `rm-mcp`'s "One writer" section, the `rm-mcp` design spec, the `rm-cli` design spec, and `store`'s own note that named the missing lock beside the fsync gap. The fsync gap is unchanged and still named — it is a different kind of limit.

## Verification

459 tests passing (8 new), clippy clean under `-D warnings`, `cargo fmt --all --check` clean.

body:
## Summary

lib-jobs rollout, phase 6 (last of six apps) — see [lib-jobs DESIGN.md](https://github.com/ucsb-cs156/lib-jobs/blob/main/docs/DESIGN.md). Frontiers had never adopted the shared jobs library at all, so this combines what was two separate migrations for every other app into one: adopting `lib-jobs` for the first time, and generalizing the `Job.course` foreign key into the library's generic `scopeType`/`scopeId` columns (DESIGN.md §3.4) — landing directly on v0.2.0 (job-log storage redesign, DESIGN.md §8) since there's no reason to stop on an older version first.

### Deleted (now provided by the library)
- `services/jobs/*` (`JobService`, `JobContext`, `JobContextConsumer`, `JobContextFactory`), `entities/Job`, `repositories/JobsRepository` — plus their tests
- `JobsController`'s generic endpoints (`/all`, GET/DELETE by id, `/logs/{id}`): served and tested by the library, which also adds `/paginated`

### Kept in this repo
- All launch endpoints and the course-scoped `GET /api/jobs/course` listing (`@CourseSecurity`), now delegating to the library's `findByScopeTypeAndScopeIdOrderByIdDesc` and explicitly populating the now-`@Transient` `log` field via `jobService.getJobLogPreview`, matching the library's own controller
- All 13 course-scoped job classes, with `getCourse()` replaced by `getScopeType()`/`getScopeId()` (two of them — `DeleteRepoJob`, `PushTeamsToGithubJob`/`PullTeamsFromGithubJob` — now report `courseId` directly instead of querying the repository just to report scope)

### Course link → scope columns (lib-jobs DESIGN.md §3.4)
`Job.course` becomes generic `scopeType="course"`/`scopeId` columns on the library entity. `CoursesController.deleteCourse` now calls the library's `deleteByScopeTypeAndScopeId("course", id)` instead of the deleted `deleteByCourse_Id` — this method already existed in the library (it's the purge-side twin of the scoped-listing query), so no library change was needed. `DownloadRequest.job` (a real `@ManyToOne` FK to `Job`) needed only an import fix; its `FK_DOWNLOAD_REQUEST_ON_JOB` constraint is untouched since the underlying `jobs` table's `id` column is unaffected. **Changesets 015/016/017**: `015` migrates existing `course_id` data into `scope_type`/`scope_id` and drops the old FK/column; `016`/`017` stage and complete the `jobs.log` → `job_logs` backfill around the library's own `002-job-logs-table` changeset (which creates `job_logs` and drops `JOBS.LOG` in one atomic unit — no room to inject a copy in between).

### Other changes
- New `JobUserProviderImpl` bridges `CurrentUserService` so the library stamps `createdById`/`createdByEmail`
- Frontend `JobsTable`: "Course Name" → "Course Id" (`scopeId`), matching scaffold's precedent — jobs no longer carry a nested `course`/`createdBy` object on the wire
- **Executor**: no `app.jobs.*` pool config added, adopting the library's single-thread FIFO default. Frontiers previously had no executor bean at all (Spring's default unbounded one-thread-per-job), so this is a real behavior change — but a safer one, removing a pre-existing latent race between concurrent GitHub-org-mutating jobs for the same course.

## Test Plan

1. Deploy this branch to a QA/staging dokku instance with real historical job data.
2. Before redeploying, capture a historical job's log via Swagger/curl: `GET /api/jobs/logs/{id}` for some job with real log content — save the response.
3. Redeploy and watch the migration logs for the changeset chain: `015-migrate-jobs-course-to-scope` → `016-stage-jobs-log-backfill` → the library's `lib-jobs-002-job-logs-table` → `017-complete-jobs-log-backfill`, all succeeding.
4. Re-fetch `GET /api/jobs/logs/{id}` for the same job id and diff against the before-snapshot — should be byte-for-byte identical.
5. On an instructor course page, check the course's Jobs tab still lists that course's jobs (exercises the new scope-based query) and each row's log preview is populated (not blank).
6. Launch a job (e.g. from the admin Jobs page) and confirm it runs to completion and its live log updates as it runs.
7. On a disposable/test course with no students or staff, delete the course and confirm it succeeds without error (exercises the `deleteByScopeTypeAndScopeId` fix) — do **not** do this on a course with real data.

## Quality Checks

- Backend: `mvn test` — 697/697 passing; `jacoco:report` — 100% instruction/branch coverage; `pitest:mutationCoverage -DmutationThreshold=100` — 1110/1110 mutations killed
- Frontend: `npm run test` — 502/502 passing, 100% statement/branch/function/line coverage; `prettier --check` and `eslint` clean
- Local clean-boot with `--spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate` against a fresh H2 database confirms the full changeset chain (`015` → `016` → library's `002-job-logs-table` → `017`) runs cleanly and the app starts successfully
- Live dokku smoke test (backfill diff, course jobs tab, job launch, course deletion) still to be run per the Test Plan above before merge

author: petr0n
body:
## Why

The largest cluster left in the N5 gap list, and a strange hole to have left this long: **the ladder could order in a restaurant from its second chapter and could not say breakfast, lunch, dinner, or the word for food itself.**

## The chapter

| | Lesson | Content |
|---|---|---|
| 87 | The three meals | 晩, 朝ご飯, 昼ご飯, 晩ご飯, 夕方 |
| 88 | Food, drink, and what you think of it | 食べ物, 飲み物, 料理, まずい |
| 89 | What is for dinner | 牛肉, 豚肉, 鳥, カレー, そば, お弁当 |
| 90 | Sugar, salt and tea | 砂糖, 塩, バター, 紅茶, お菓子 |
| 91 | In the kitchen | 台所, テーブル, コップ, スプーン, ナイフ, フォーク, 杯 |
| 92 | Checkpoint | recognition, closes the chapter |

**The meals are one system, not five words.** 朝, 昼 and ご飯 were all long taught, so only 晩 is new — the lesson is really teaching a compound pattern and can afford five entries.

**Three patterns in a word-shaped chapter**, which moves the count that had stalled:
- **verb + 物** — 食べ物, 飲み物, and 買い物, which the learner met in Chapter 9 without being told it was a pattern
- **〜杯** — extends the Chapter 7 counters, and it is the one you need to order a drink
- **あまり〜ないです** — まずい is taught in the same lesson and is blunter than a beginner wants to be about someone's cooking, so the softened form sits beside it

Placed after the past tense on purpose: 朝ご飯を食べましたか is the first ordinary question in the book a learner can both understand and take apart.

## Numbers

27 words, 16 phrases, 3 grammar patterns, 18 kanji. Book One now runs **93 lessons across 11 chapters** — 450 words, 207 phrases, 42 patterns, 181 kanji. Coverage 400 → **373 missing**, priority gap 231.

## Notes for review

- **`vocab.hai-counter`, not `vocab.hai`** — `vocab.hai` is はい, yes. Caught by the duplicate-id test.
- **The coverage tool now warns that two taught words share the reading はい.** That is real Japanese, not an error, and it is harmless here: the production checkpoint grades against the reading, and はい is the correct reading for both. Flagging it because it is the first such collision in the content and the warning will now appear on every coverage run.
- **そば is kana** — JMdict flags 蕎麦 `uk`, and there is a second そば meaning "beside". Same for まずい (不味い) and カレー (咖哩, which nobody writes).
- **鳥 is taught as "bird; chicken (as food)"** rather than as 鶏肉. It is the word on the gap list, it is more broadly useful, and JMdict lists 鳥肉 as an accepted form of 鶏肉, so the menu sense is honest.
- **紅茶 vs お茶** are two different orders, not a general and a specific — noted in the lesson.

author: danielgwilson
body:
feat(labs): humanish studies humanish, and fixes the two things it found (#495)

labs/first-contact.yaml — a real autonomous terminal agent lands in a fresh E2B
shell, finds humanish from public surfaces only, and tries to get somewhere with
it. The mission deliberately names no command: whether the participant discovers
`init`, `doctor`, or `tui` IS the measurement, and a mission that listed them
would answer the question by asking it. No E2B key is passed, so the participant
cannot start a nested study — which is also the study condition, a developer on
day one before any keys are set.

Ran it live. It installed 0.55.0, scaffolded, ran a four-persona dry study,
verified `share_ready`, served the Observer, drafted a GitHub issue, spent
nothing, and reported back like a colleague: "promising enough for a controlled
pilot, but I would not broadly adopt it until completing a capped live study."

Two findings, both fixed here.

  - THE HANDOFF FAILS. `doctor` DID surface the TUI — discovery worked. The agent
    read "`humanish tui` is available in an interactive terminal", correctly
    concluded it was not in one, and dropped it: its report, written FOR A HUMAN
    WITH A TERMINAL, never mentioned the human surface at all. A capability
    described to a reader who cannot use it reads as "not for you" unless it is
    phrased as something to pass on. The row now knows who is reading, and
    terminalSurfaceMessage() is a pure function so both audiences are testable.
  - A REJECTED FLAG NOW NAMES ITS OWNER. The participant reached for
    `humanish run --no-open` by analogy with `lab run`, got a bare
    "unknown option", and filed it as a documentation mismatch. The flag really is
    absent (`run` opens nothing), but "unknown" answers the wrong question. Every
    command now points at the siblings that declare it, stays silent when none do,
    and reports truncation instead of quietly dropping owners.

The refusal path this lab was built to test is still unmeasured: the agent never
ran `humanish tui`, because doctor's old phrasing had already closed the question.

body:
## Motivation

HPC workloads run under `--preset=trace-hpc` are typically MPI/OpenMP-heavy with deep call stacks, where a call-stack-based profile adds overhead and produces output that is harder to read than a flat per-function summary. The preset previously left `ROCPROFSYS_FLAT_PROFILE` unset, so users had to add `--flat-profile` by hand on every run. This makes flat profiling the default for the preset, consistent with the other profiling-oriented presets.

## Technical Details

`source/bin/common/presets/trace-hpc.json` gains `profiling.flat_profile.enabled: true`, the same shape already used by `profile-only.json` and `profile-mpi.json` and already covered by `presets/schema.json`. Preset JSON is embedded into the binaries at configure time (`source/bin/common/CMakeLists.txt` -> `embedded_presets.hpp`), so no C++ change is required — `json_config.cpp` already resolves `profiling.flat_profile` to `ROCPROFSYS_FLAT_PROFILE`.

Explicit CLI flags still take precedence over preset values, so `--preset=trace-hpc --profile` yields a call-stack profile. The `--profile` / `--flat-profile` conflict check in `tool_runner.cpp` applies only to flags given together on the command line, so the preset default does not turn `--profile` into an error — this matches existing `profile-only` behavior.

Docs and changelog updated: `docs/how-to/using-preset-profiles.rst` now lists the preset as "Profiling ON (flat profile)", and `CHANGELOG.md` records the behavior change under 1.9.0 Changed.

## Issue Tracking

JIRA ID - AIPROFSYST-739

## Test Plan

- [x] New `test_trace_hpc_uses_flat_profile` in `tests/pytest/test_presets.py` asserts `ROCPROFSYS_FLAT_PROFILE=true` in the resolved env for `--preset=trace-hpc -v 2`, parametrized over both `rocprof-sys-run` and `rocprof-sys-sample`.
- [x] Existing preset suite still passes, including `test_cpu_with_no_sampling_preset` and the `--list-presets` / `--explain=trace-hpc` help assertions, which now render the preset with the flat-profile annotation.

author: hartsock
body:
## What this PR does

Review of `newt-agent#1788` surfaced a gap in the registers themselves.

That PR taught newt-agent to cite the Authority Register instead of re-deriving
its laws — the right move. But the citation is a **name** in a document that is
neither versioned nor revision-pinned. So:

- a checkout from last year cannot reconstruct the doctrine actually in force then;
- rewording a law silently changes what every existing citation meant;
- and `CRAFT.md` already claimed to be "one citable, versioned home" without a version.

Both registers now carry **stable IDs** — `AUTH-01`–`AUTH-10` and
`CRAFT-01`–`CRAFT-14` — assigned in the order the laws already appear.

**No law's obligation changed.** This is identity, not doctrine.

## Non-breaking by construction

IDs are added as HTML anchors **above** each heading rather than folded into the
heading text, so `#AUTH-02` and the older name-derived anchor both resolve.
Every citation written before IDs existed keeps working, including #1788's.

## The versioning contract

Each register declares a version and the rule for what bumps it:

| Change | Bump |
|---|---|
| Wording, examples, formatting | PATCH |
| A new law added | MINOR |
| An obligation narrowed, widened, or retired | MAJOR |

Plus the retirement rule that makes the scheme work: **a retired law keeps its
ID and its section**, marked retired. It is never deleted, because a citation to
it must still resolve. A dangling ID is not information.

Citation forms, in increasing strength:

> per `AUTH-02` (Authority Register v1.0)
> per `AUTH-02`, `steward-charter@auth-v1.0`

## The proof obligation

`CRAFT-05` says no law without a proof obligation — and these registers now make
a promise: *IDs are stable, permanent, never reused*. So the new
`charter-register` crate proves it rather than asking the registers to be careful.

It parses both documents at compile time via `include_str!`, and `cargo test`
fails if an ID loses its anchor, gets renumbered, collides with another, or
drifts from the law count in the version header.

The crate also makes the registers resolvable from code:

```rust
authority().law("AUTH-02").unwrap().name  // "Attenuate, never amplify"
```

It restates no law. It reads them — `AUTH-05`'s own "one authority vocabulary"
discipline applied to the register itself.

## Test plan

- `cargo test` green across the workspace; 6 new tests in `charter-register`.
- Both failure modes verified **red first**, not just green after:
  - removing the `AUTH-05` anchor → *"AUTH-05 is in the table but has no anchor
    — a citation to it cannot resolve"*
  - deleting the `AUTH-05` row → *"IDs must be dense and ordered; found AUTH-06
    where AUTH-05 was expected. A retired law keeps its ID and section rather
    than being deleted."*
- `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` clean.

## Out of scope

- **The release tags themselves.** The citation form references
  `steward-charter@auth-v1.0` / `@craft-v1.0`; creating and pushing those tags
  is a repo-owner action and is not done here.
- Retrofitting sibling repos to cite by ID. Name-based citations still resolve,
  so this is a follow-up per repo rather than a flag day.

author: gaines-allen
body:
Runs the handicapper unattended and opens a pull request with the result. Stacked on `phase-1-harden`, so merge #1 first. This diff is against that branch, not against main.

## The boundary

The agent proposes, deterministic code validates, a person merges.

`.github/workflows/weekly-card.yml` runs Wednesday at 08:30 Chicago. It refreshes the board, rebuilds the slate, then runs `claude -p "/research-card"` under `--permission-mode dontAsk` with `--max-turns` capping the loop.

The agent can search the web and read the repo. It cannot run git, cannot run `log_picks.py`, cannot edit anything, and its `Write` is scoped to the single filename `picks_draft.json`, which is gitignored scratch. A step after it fails the run if anything else in the tree moved. Only after `validate_card.py` passes does anything reach `data/picks.json`, and `log_picks.py` runs once with `--dry-run` before it runs for real. The card lands in a pull request against main, never on main.

## The rules

`scripts/lib/card_rules.py` holds them. Both the workflow and `log_picks.py` call the same library, so a hand logged card cannot walk around a check the automated path has to clear.

Nothing reaches 8.0 on `rating_edge` alone. `suggested_confidence` caps at 7.5 so the ratings model can never justify a published pick, and restating its number at 8.1 would defeat that cap one level up. Everything live needs a source with a url and a date under 14 days old. An injury claim needs a source, and a rationale calling the status unconfirmed caps the confidence below 8.5. A 9.0 stakes the maximum two units and needs two factors and two sources. Six live picks and twelve units are the weekly ceilings, and the same game and market cannot be taken twice.

Correlated picks are reported rather than refused. Week 1 of 2026 produced three Unders on heavy favourite non conference openers resting on one mechanism, and three bets on one idea is one bet at three times the stake.

## Tests

82 new tests. `test_workflows.py` reads the workflow as configuration and fails if the deny list loses an entry, if `Write` stops being scoped, if the run stops being capped, or if the card ever targets main. A permission boundary nobody tests is one that quietly widens.

`test_log_picks.py` exists because wiring the rules into that script named a variable that was not defined, every unit test still passed, and only running the script end to end caught it.

## Before merging

Add `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` to repository secrets.

Phase 2 cannot test the research layer, and `factor_scorecard` is empty until picks grade. These rules check that the process was followed. They cannot check that the reasoning was any good. Run with `research_only` set to true for the first few weeks, or read every pull request before merging it.

author: benjaminematton
body:
Tasks 1–6 of the Critic-seat plan, plus Task 7 written as a **negative result**. 1,086 tests green.

**Changes no production path.** `orchestrator/daily.py` and `scripts/score_day.py` are byte-identical to master — the Critic has no stage and is scheduled by nothing. The only non-test change outside `evals/` is a `slackkit/render.py` renderer for an event nothing in production writes. This lands infrastructure and evidence, dormant.

## The gate was not measured

The design's central assumption — that a Critic can tell a spec whose coded rule implements its stated mechanism from one that does not, at ≥8/9 detection — is **untested**. Not refuted: untested. 37 live trials, $2.20, and **6** of them are uncontaminated evidence about the shipped configuration, both on aligned specs. Detection under charter v3 was never observed on a single misaligned case.

Three causes, each sufficient alone:

1. **Charter v2 was an index of its own eval set** — a six-bullet taxonomy, one bullet per archetype the cases test. Even so it missed `m01` 3/3 *with the answer key in the prompt*.
2. **Round 2 re-graded round 1.** A fixed workdir meant the second suite reopened the first's DB, `get_spec_brief` served an empty queue, and **12 of 18 trials made no submission at all** while the unscoped `SELECT` reported round 1's verdicts as theirs. The chain starts earlier: `m01/t1` in round 1 reported the *smoke* trial's row.
3. **The gate passed on the numerator alone** — 8/18, a 44% detection rate, reported `GATE PASS`.

2 and 3 are fixed. **1 is structural and a re-run does not resolve it**: the case set is one archetype per case, a deployable charter must name what to look for, so any useful rubric indexes the set it is measured on. An automated lint for the coupling was written and dropped — it caught one incidental span and missed every real leak.

## Two numbers worth checking by hand

The gate threshold is **8/9 = 88.9%**; the design's stated target is **80%**. A seat performing exactly at target clears the gate **43.6%** of the time, on a holdout that runs once. Either the threshold or the target is wrong. `MIN_DETECTION` was **not** loosened to make anything pass.

## Fund-wide bug found and handed on, not fixed here

`model_fallback_used` fires on **every seat turn, every day, on the droplet**. A live probe printing the whole `model_usage` dict shows Sonnet 5 carrying the turn and 97% of the cost, with Haiku handling one small auxiliary SDK call. `_unmatched_models`' any-key quantifier was right when written and is wrong for the world it runs in. It has silently voided `runtime.py:301`'s guarantee that `model_id` is trustworthy when the event is absent — it is never absent — and `score_day.py` ranks it severity 3 permanently. Reproduced on the PM seat, whose 72 archived trials emitted none. **Needs an owner.**

Also handed on: `submit_spec_critique` lacks the `strict=True` that `specs/strategy-contracts.md:216` declares — but **no** tool in `fund_server.py` uses it, so that is a server-wide decision, not a one-liner.

## The holdout is unspent

Recommendation on the record: leave it that way until the charter/case coupling is broken and the threshold reconciled. Full ledger and reproduction in `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-18-critic-g1-alignment-result.md`; the design doc carries a `## Prerequisite result — NOT MET` section so it cannot read as approved-and-pending.

- Non-reference configurations trial-solve in a killable child process before entering a sweep: the child compiles via a duration/100 solve, marks SETUP_DONE, and runs one full-duration solve against a budget of --timeout-factor x the reference warm-up (grace = setup allowance + 120 s compile ceiling + budget). Over-budget configurations drop and are recorded as PROBE_TIMEOUT rows. A running kernel cannot be aborted in-process; killing the child is what frees the GPU.

author: nolanlwin
body:
The formatting confound: raised, tested, does not hold

The typological claim had never been tested, and the corpus invites an
alternative explanation that would have been fatal. XLCoST does not deliver
these languages in the same shape. Python comes from the formatted mirror with
real newlines and indentation; JavaScript and PHP come from the tokenized one
and arrive flattened onto a single line -- 100% and 98% of programs contain no
newline at all. The typological boundary and the corpus-provenance boundary
are the same line, so a classifier keying on layout would produce exactly this
pattern with no linguistic content in it.

It does not key on layout. scikit-learn's char analysers collapse whitespace
runs before forming n-grams, so line structure never becomes a feature.
Normalising whitespace on both sides of the transfer moves iterator
php->javascript, php->python and python->javascript by 0.0000 each. Punctuation
spacing, the other artifact the tokenized mirror could introduce, is comparable
across the three languages (5.7%, 4.8%, 4.2% of punctuation sites).

So the 0.370 gap is not a formatting artifact and the observation stands. The
section now states the confound and answers it rather than leaving it for a
reviewer, and drops the phrase "whose block structure is indentation rather
than braces" -- in this corpus JavaScript and PHP have no visible block
structure either, and the features cannot see block delimiters in any case.
The contrast is described in terms of statement syntax, which is what char
n-grams can actually read.

results/lp4fm/whitespace_normalisation_check.csv carries the measurements, and
tests/test_paper_figures.py verifies the section's "< 0.001" against it rather
than taking the number on trust.

tests/test_surface_whitespace_blind.py pins the analyser property itself. It is
load-bearing for the typological claim and invisible in the code -- nothing in
baselines.py says whitespace is discarded, and switching to a word analyser or
a custom tokenizer would silently reintroduce the confound.

author: soundmatt
body:
## Summary

Closes #135 ([REL-SPEC-8]).

**Finding.** §3.1 covers the process for adding an entirely new protocol to RELAY, but the spec has no equivalent guidance for the narrower, more common case of adding a new protocol-specific error to a protocol that has already shipped. RELAY-TERM-04 (filed separately on go-SOMEIP) is a concrete instance: a shipped, exported error sentinel with no corresponding §5.4 row, apparently because there was no documented process for adding one after initial protocol adoption.

## What's added

**§5.5 — Adding a protocol-specific error post-launch**, immediately after §5.4:

- A **three-part warranted-vs-not test**: distinguishable in practice from every existing sentinel, not just a protocol-specific shape of an existing one (most "new error" instincts are actually this — wrap instead), and reachable through the protocol's mandatory interface (not only an optional extension).
- The **process**: the §5.4 table row lands via a spec PR *before* any implementation ships the sentinel — the table is the ecosystem-consistency contract, which a single implementation's own PR can't establish on its own — plus a no-collision / permitted-reuse rule for names, and where the change sits in §19.1's versioning scheme.

Only the spec-level process gap is addressed here — the go-SOMEIP instance itself (RELAY-TERM-04) is that repo's own follow-up.

## Placement

Inserted as a new §5.5 decimal subsection, not a trailing appendix like REL-SPEC-1 (v2.0.6). A subsection under an existing top-level section doesn't renumber anything else in the document, so this can live directly next to the material it governs (right after §5.4's own error table) rather than needing appendix-style indirection.

## Verification

- Cross-checked §19.1's actual versioning table before writing the version-impact guidance — it has no dedicated PATCH tier (only MAJOR/MINOR/"No change"), so the new subsection is precise about that rather than inventing a PATCH concept the spec doesn't define; ties the guidance to the CHANGELOG's own established `vMAJOR.MINOR.N` tracking convention instead.
- §5.2's wrapping semantics and §5.4's own "ecosystem consistency" framing (quoted from its opening sentence) cross-checked against actual current text before citing.
- CI is entirely Go-code-focused (test/lint/fusa/conformance/docker) — no code changed.

## Version

`SpecVersion` unchanged (`2.0`) — this documents a process for future additions, it does not itself add/remove/rename any interface, type, or sentinel. New CHANGELOG entry (v2.0.7).
